body_text: Enterprise contract establishes a streamlined path for Army and joint-force units to deploy Rune’s TyrOS platform. ARLINGTON, Va. — June 18, 2026 — Rune Technologies, which builds AI-enabled predictive software for military logistics in contested environments, today announced a five-year, $99 million Indefinite Delivery, Indefinite Quantity (IDIQ) contract with the U.S. Army. The contract establishes an enterprise acquisition vehicle that enables U.S. Army organizations, other Department of War components, and joint force partners, to rapidly procure Rune's TyrOS platform and associated services through streamlined task orders. The contract creates a centralized pathway for Department of War organizations to acquire modern commercial software capabilities that improve operational readiness, logistics, autonomy, command and control, resource visibility, and decision-making across contested and distributed environments. Established by the Army and available for broader DoW use, the vehicle enables Soldiers, Marines, Sailors, Airmen, Guardians, Commanders, Sustainers, acquisition professionals, and contracting teams to rapidly access and field proven software solutions at the speed of operations. Under the IDIQ structure, authorized Department of War organizations can procure TyrOS and associated services through task orders issued against the contract throughout the five-year period of performance. Each order provides a streamlined path to procure and field TyrOS without initiating a separate and new competitive contracting action, reducing acquisition timelines from months to days. The vehicle is designed to scale alongside operational demand, enabling the rapid expansion of software capabilities across the Joint Force. As near-peer adversaries develop the ability to disrupt supply lines and communications, commanders need systems that can track assets, anticipate shortfalls, and recommend courses of action even when connectivity fails. TyrOS’s edge-first architecture puts intelligence at the tactical level, where decisions are made. "Logistics is the distribution layer of military power, and it has to move at the speed of the fight," said David Tuttle, Co-Founder and CEO of Rune Technologies . “This contract gives sustainment teams across the Army and joint force a single, repeatable way to deploy TyrOS and other Rune capabilities into their units, while reducing acquisition friction and accelerating capability delivery to the tactical edge.” The award builds on a year of accelerating adoption for Rune across the Joint Force. The company recently launched Saga, their Agentic Logistician, an AI agent built on TyrOS that condenses days of logistics planning into seconds, and their Autonomy Development Kit to accelerate the distribution, scheduling and tasking of autonomous systems as part of a sustainment orchestration layer. Rune has deployed TyrOS across Army and Marine Corps operational formations, including the 25th Infantry Division, 4th Infantry Division, XVIII Airborne Corps, and the U.S. Marine Corps Warfighting Laboratory. The company currently supports both Army NGC2 modernization efforts and Marine Corps Project Dynamis experimentation, bringing AI-enabled sustainment and mission command capabilities to emerging Joint Force concepts. To learn more about TyrOS and Rune Technologies, visit runetech.co . About Rune Technologies: Rune Technologies is revolutionizing military logistics through AI-enabled predictive software that operates in contested environments where communications are denied or degraded. Rune's TyrOS platform transforms manual logistics processes into intelligent supply webs that anticipate needs, optimize resources, and enable distributed operations at machine speed, even when supply lines are targeted by near-peer adversaries. Founded by veterans with deep operational experience and Silicon Valley engineering talent, Rune is ensuring military effectiveness through precise execution of critical logistics operations. For more information, visit runetech.co . Media Contact: Sam Polstein rune@deeptech.agency

title: 7 B2B Lead Generation Strategies That Actually Work
summary: Uncover effective B2B lead generation strategies that drive results. Learn how to attract and convert high-quality leads with proven techniques.
body_text: B2B sales Outbound Prospecting Top of the funnel Pipeline Generation 7 B2B Lead Generation Strategies That Actually Work In a world of automated emails and impersonal outreach, making a genuine connection feels more important than ever. Your potential customers aren't just entries in a spreadsheet; they're people looking for real solutions to their business problems. The most successful B2B lead generation strategies recognize this and prioritize building relationships over simply collecting contacts. This isn't about abandoning technology, but about using it to enable more meaningful conversations. This guide is built on that philosophy. We'll explore how to combine smart tactics with a human touch to attract prospects who are genuinely a good fit, nurture them with valuable insights, and start conversations that lead to lasting partnerships. Key Takeaways Prioritize high-quality leads over high volume: A long list of unqualified prospects drains your team's time. Focus your efforts on attracting the right businesses by clearly defining your ideal customer and using personalization to show you understand their specific needs. Create a seamless experience across multiple channels: Your prospects interact with your brand in many places, from social media to their inbox. By integrating your efforts—like following up a webinar with a personalized email—you create a consistent and trustworthy brand experience that guides leads smoothly through their decision-making process. Make data-driven decisions to refine your approach: Don't guess what works—let your results guide you. Regularly track key metrics like conversion rates and sales cycle length, and use A/B testing to improve everything from email subject lines to ad copy. This commitment to continuous improvement is what turns a good strategy into a great one. What is B2B Lead Generation and Why Does It Matter? At its core, B2B lead generation is the process of identifying businesses that could benefit from your product or service and sparking their interest. A "lead" is any company that has shown potential to become a customer. This isn't about making a sale on the first call; it's the critical first step in building a relationship that guides a potential buyer from initial awareness to a signed contract. Think of it as the official start of your customer's journey with you. So, why is this process so important? Because a steady flow of quality leads is the lifeblood of any B2B company. It’s how you consistently fill your sales pipeline with new opportunities, ensuring your business has a path to predictable growth. Without a deliberate strategy to generate leads, you’re left waiting for customers to find you, which is rarely a recipe for success. A proactive approach puts you in control of your company's future. Effective lead generation is also about efficiency. A well-designed strategy doesn't just bring in more leads—it brings in the right leads. By understanding your ideal customer profile, you can focus your sales efforts on prospects who are most likely to convert. This saves your sales team valuable time and energy, allowing them to nurture promising relationships instead of chasing down cold trails. When your sales and marketing teams are aligned on who to target, the entire sales process becomes smoother, faster, and more profitable. Know Your Leads: MQLs vs. SQLs Not all leads are created equal, and knowing the difference can completely change your sales game. Let's break down the two main categories you'll hear about: Marketing Qualified Leads (MQLs) and Sales Qualified Leads (SQLs). Understanding this distinction is the first step toward building a more efficient and effective sales process. Think of an MQL as someone who has raised their hand to show they're interested in what you have to say. They might have downloaded an ebook, subscribed to your newsletter, or spent a good amount of time on your pricing page. They're curious and engaging with your marketing materials, but they haven't explicitly asked to speak with a salesperson just yet. They are in the research phase, exploring their options. An SQL, on the other hand, has moved past general curiosity and is showing clear signs they're ready to talk business. This is someone who has requested a demo, filled out a "contact sales" form, or asked specific questions about how your product could solve their unique problem. These are the leads your sales team should prioritize immediately because their actions signal a strong intent to buy. Separating your leads into these two buckets is crucial for effective lead generation. It allows your marketing team to focus on nurturing MQLs with helpful content, guiding them closer to a decision without being pushy. Meanwhile, your sales team can dedicate their valuable time to the SQLs who are most likely to convert. A great way to automate this process is by implementing lead scoring, which assigns points to leads based on their actions. Once a lead hits a certain score, they automatically transition from an MQL to an SQL, signaling that it's time for your sales team to reach out. 7 Proven B2B Lead Generation Strategies Finding the right leads is about meeting your future customers where they are and offering them something of value. It’s a mix of smart strategy, consistent effort, and genuine connection. Instead of casting a wide, generic net, these seven strategies focus on attracting, engaging, and nurturing the right people for your business. Let’s walk through some of the most effective ways to fill your pipeline with quality B2B leads. Create Valuable Content to Attract Leads Think of your content as the front door to your business. It’s often the first interaction a potential lead has with your brand. The key is to create high-quality, relevant content that solves a problem or answers a question for your ideal customer. This isn't about a hard sell; it's about building trust. When you consistently provide helpful information through blog posts, white papers, or case studies, you establish your company as an authority in your field. This approach attracts potential leads through search engines and social sharing, drawing them in because you’re offering expertise, not just a product pitch. A solid content marketing plan is the foundation for this entire strategy. Engage Your Audience on Social Media For B2B, social media is less about viral trends and more about building professional relationships. Platforms like LinkedIn are perfect for connecting directly with decision-makers in your industry. The goal is to engage, not just broadcast. Share insightful articles (both yours and others'), ask thoughtful questions to start conversations, and participate in relevant groups. By actively engaging, you can build a community around your brand and keep your business top-of-mind. When a need arises, those connections you’ve nurtured are more likely to think of you first. This consistent, authentic interaction turns your social profiles into powerful lead-generation tools. Nurture Leads with Email Campaigns Once you have a lead’s contact information, the conversation is just beginning. Email marketing is your direct line to nurturing that new relationship. The trick is to guide them with valuable information, not bombard them with sales pitches. You can set up automated email marketing sequences that deliver helpful content, customer stories, and exclusive insights over time. Each email should build on the last, gently moving the lead through your sales funnel by addressing their potential pain points and demonstrating how you can help. This methodical approach builds trust and prepares them for a more direct sales conversation when the time is right. Build Relationships Through Networking Never underestimate the power of a personal connection. Building a strong professional network, both online and in person, is a cornerstone of B2B lead generation. Actively participate in industry forums, attend conferences, and connect with peers on LinkedIn. The goal isn't to collect business cards but to build genuine relationships. These connections can lead to direct business and, just as importantly, referrals. A recommendation from a trusted peer is one of the most powerful leads you can get. By investing time in building your network, you create a sustainable source of high-quality opportunities that grow over time. Optimize Your Online Presence with SEO Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is how you ensure that when your ideal customer searches for a solution on Google, they find you. It’s the technical backbone that supports your content strategy. By optimizing your website and content with the keywords your audience is using, you improve your visibility in search results. This isn't just about stuffing keywords into a page; it's about creating a great user experience and structuring your site so search engines understand what you're about. Good B2B SEO makes you discoverable at the exact moment a potential lead is looking for help, bringing qualified traffic directly to your digital doorstep. Target Ideal Customers with Paid Ads While organic strategies build momentum over time, paid advertising can deliver immediate results. Platforms like Google Ads and LinkedIn Ads allow you to get your message in front of a highly specific audience. You can target users based on job title, industry, company size, and online behavior, ensuring your budget is spent on reaching the most relevant prospects. A well-designed ad campaign can quickly generate leads, test messaging, and drive traffic to a landing page built for conversions. It’s a fantastic way to supplement your organic efforts and reach potential customers who may not have found you otherwise. Showcase Your Expertise with Webinars and Events Hosting a webinar or a virtual event is one of the best ways to generate high-intent leads. It gives you a platform to dive deep into a topic, demonstrate your expertise, and interact with your audience in real time. By offering a free, educational session, you provide immense value in exchange for a lead's contact information. These aren't just any leads; they are people who have actively set aside time to learn from you, signaling a strong interest in what you have to offer. Hosting a webinar allows you to educate a captive audience and directly answer their questions, building a powerful case for your solution. Use Technology to Generate B2B Leads Generating a steady stream of B2B leads requires more than just great strategy—it demands the right tools to execute it effectively. Technology is your partner in this process, helping you work smarter, not harder. When you have the right systems in place, you can scale your outreach, personalize your communication, and keep your entire team on the same page without letting important details slip through the cracks. A well-chosen tech stack doesn’t replace the human element of sales; it enhances it by handling the heavy lifting so your team can focus on what they do best: building relationships and closing deals. Think of your technology as the foundation of your lead generation house. Without a solid base, everything else becomes wobbly and inefficient. The three essential pillars of this foundation are a customer relationship management (CRM) system to keep your data organized, automation tools to streamline your workflows, and analytics platforms to measure what’s working. By integrating these technologies into your daily operations, you create a powerful engine for growth that consistently attracts, nurtures, and converts high-quality leads for your business. This isn't about buying every shiny new tool on the market, but about strategically choosing platforms that solve specific problems and work together seamlessly. Organize and Manage Leads with a CRM If your lead information is scattered across spreadsheets, inboxes, and sticky notes, it’s time for a central hub. A Customer Relationship Management (CRM) system is the single source of truth for all your prospect and customer data. Using a CRM to manage leads is crucial because it helps you track every interaction, from the first email they opened to the last call they had with your sales team. This detailed history gives you a complete picture of each lead’s journey, allowing you to have more relevant and timely conversations. A well-implemented CRM streamlines your entire process, ensuring no lead is forgotten and every opportunity is followed up on. It empowers your team with the context they need to nurture relationships effectively and turn interested prospects into loyal customers. Streamline Your Process with Automation Imagine getting back all the hours your team spends on repetitive, manual tasks. That’s the power of automation. Marketing automation platforms can handle everything from sending welcome email sequences to posting on social media, freeing up your team to focus on high-value activities that require a human touch. By automating these routine tasks, you can nurture leads more efficiently and at a much larger scale. The goal of marketing automation isn’t to create a robotic experience; it’s to deliver the right message to the right person at the right time. You can set up triggers that send personalized content based on a lead’s behavior, ensuring your communication is always relevant. This keeps your brand top-of-mind and warms up leads so they are more receptive when a salesperson finally reaches out. Make Data-Driven Decisions with Analytics Guesswork has no place in a successful lead generation strategy. To make smart decisions, you need to rely on data. Utilizing website analytics to track traffic, user behavior, and conversion rates is essential for understanding what’s resonating with your audience and what’s falling flat. This information is a goldmine for refining your approach over time. By analyzing your data, you can answer critical questions: Which blog posts are generating the most qualified leads? Which marketing channels are delivering the best return on investment? Where are users dropping off in your conversion funnel? Tools like Google Analytics help you identify these patterns, allowing you to double down on what works and fix what doesn’t. This cycle of analysis and optimization is the key to building a lead generation machine that improves continuously. How to Measure Your Lead Generation Success Once your lead generation engine is running, you need a way to see what’s working and what isn’t. Measuring your success isn't just about counting the number of new contacts in your CRM. It’s about understanding the quality of those leads, the efficiency of your process, and the ultimate impact on your bottom line. Without clear metrics, you’re essentially flying blind, pouring resources into channels that might not be delivering real value. Tracking the right key performance indicators (KPIs) helps you make informed, data-driven decisions. You can double down on the strategies that bring in high-quality prospects and tweak or abandon the ones that don’t. This is how you refine your approach over time, ensuring your sales and marketing efforts are as effective as possible. Let’s walk through the essential metrics you should be monitoring to get a complete picture of your lead generation performance. Track Lead Progress with Conversion Rates Conversion rates tell you how effectively your leads are moving through your sales funnel. One of the most important metrics to watch is your lead-to-opportunity rate, which shows the percentage of leads that your sales team deems qualified enough to pursue. This is a direct reflection of your lead quality. If this number is low, it might mean your marketing messages are attracting the wrong audience. On average, this rate is around 12% for B2B companies, so you can use that as a starting benchmark. Tracking this helps you gauge whether your initial targeting and qualification criteria are on point. Evaluate ROI with Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) Your Customer Acquisition Cost (CAC) is the total amount you spend on sales and marketing to acquire a new customer. To calculate it, you simply divide your total campaign costs by the number of new customers you gained from that campaign. This metric is fundamental to understanding your return on investment (ROI). Surprisingly, research shows that only 21% of B2B marketers feel confident in their ability to track ROI, which leaves a huge opportunity for improvement. A lower CAC is great, but it’s most meaningful when compared to the lifetime value (LTV) of your customers. A healthy business model ensures your LTV is significantly higher than your CAC. Assess the Value of Your Leads It’s easy to fall into the trap of thinking that more leads automatically equals more success. However, one of the biggest misconceptions about lead generation is that it’s purely a numbers game. The truth is, lead quality trumps quantity every time. A hundred lukewarm leads who aren’t a good fit for your product will drain your sales team’s time and energy. Ten highly qualified leads who are genuinely interested in your solution are far more valuable. Focus on metrics that reflect lead quality, like the conversion rates we just discussed, to ensure your team is spending its time on prospects who are likely to become happy customers. Find Efficiencies by Tracking Sales Cycle Length The sales cycle length is the average time it takes for a lead to become a customer. A shorter sales cycle is generally a sign of an efficient process and high-quality leads who are ready to make a decision. If your sales cycle is dragging on, it could indicate a few things: your leads might not be properly qualified, there could be bottlenecks in your sales process, or your nurturing campaigns might need some work. Since every B2B sales strategy is unique to the business and industry, there’s no universal "right" length. The key is to track your own average and look for ways to shorten it without sacrificing the customer experience. How to Overcome Common Lead Generation Challenges Even the most well-oiled lead generation machine hits a few bumps in the road. It’s completely normal to face challenges like inconsistent lead quality or a disconnect between your teams. The key is to recognize these hurdles and have a plan to address them head-on. By focusing on alignment, quality, and adaptability, you can build a more resilient and effective lead generation strategy that consistently delivers results. Align Your Sales and Marketing Teams One of the most common roadblocks to effective lead generation is a gap between sales and marketing. When these two teams operate in silos, you end up with marketing sending over leads that sales can't close. The fix? Get them on the same page. When both teams work together, they can create a unified strategy that targets the right audience and improves conversion rates. Start by establishing a shared definition of a "qualified lead" and hold regular meetings to review goals, discuss feedback, and celebrate wins. This collaboration ensures everyone is pulling in the same direction, turning marketing efforts into tangible revenue. Maintain Consistent Lead Quality It’s easy to get caught up in the numbers game, but a long list of unqualified leads won’t do your sales team any favors. To maintain consistent lead quality, you have to be disciplined about your targeting and data management. This means regularly refining your ideal customer profile and ensuring your data is clean and accurate. Take a close look at your analytics to see which channels and campaigns are bringing in the highest-quality leads, and double down on what works. Prioritizing quality over sheer quantity helps your sales team focus their energy where it counts, leading to better conversion rates and a healthier bottom line. Adapt to Changing Market Conditions The B2B landscape is anything but static. Customer needs evolve, new competitors emerge, and economic shifts can change the game overnight. Staying successful requires you to be agile. Adapting to changing market conditions is essential for keeping your lead generation efforts relevant and effective. Make it a habit to monitor industry trends, listen to what your customers are saying, and keep an eye on your competitors. This awareness allows you to pivot your messaging, explore new channels, and adjust your strategy quickly, ensuring you continue to connect with your target audience in a meaningful way. Find the Right Balance Between Lead Quality and Quantity The pressure to fill the sales pipeline is real, but focusing only on quantity can quickly burn out your team with low-quality leads. Finding the right balance is a common challenge, but it's critical for sustainable growth. A strategic approach that emphasizes nurturing high-quality prospects while maintaining a healthy pipeline is the key to long-term success. Implementing a lead scoring system can help your team prioritize their efforts on the leads most likely to convert. This allows you to dedicate the right resources to the right prospects without letting the top of your funnel run dry. Personalize Your Outreach for Better Results If you want to stand out in a crowded inbox, a generic, one-size-fits-all message won’t cut it. Your prospects are busy, and they can spot a formulaic email blast from a mile away. Personalization is about making your outreach genuinely relevant to the person on the other end. It goes far beyond just using their first name; it’s about showing you’ve done your homework and understand their specific business challenges and goals. This approach signals that you value their time and see them as a potential partner, not just another number on a list. When you tailor your outreach, you’re not just trying to get a response—you’re starting a real conversation. This builds a foundation of trust from the very first interaction, making prospects much more likely to engage with you. Meaningful connections begin with genuine, personalized communication that addresses what your prospect actually cares about. It’s the difference between being ignored and being seen as a valuable resource. Tailor Your Approach to Each Prospect Before you hit send or pick up the phone, take a few minutes to research your prospect. Look at their LinkedIn profile, their company’s website, and any recent news or press releases. What are their responsibilities? What are their company’s current priorities? This small investment of time pays off significantly. By understanding the specific pain points and goals of each prospect, you can craft messages that resonate and encourage action. Mentioning a recent company achievement or a shared connection shows you’ve put in the effort. This tailored approach helps you build rapport and proves you’re offering a thoughtful solution, not just a generic product. Use Data to Inform Your Personalization Strategy Personalizing every single message by hand isn't always practical, especially as you scale. This is where data becomes your most valuable asset. Your CRM, website analytics, and past customer interactions are full of insights. By analyzing this information, you can identify patterns in customer behavior and preferences. This allows you to segment your audience into smaller, more specific groups based on factors like industry, job title, or past engagement. This data-driven approach lets you send highly relevant, targeted campaigns that feel personal even when they’re automated, leading to more effective outreach and stronger connections from the start. Combine Your Channels for Maximum Impact Your leads don't live in a single channel, so your marketing shouldn't either. Think about the last time you made a significant business purchase. You probably saw an ad, read a blog post, received an email, and maybe even spoke to someone on the phone. Each of these touchpoints played a role in your decision. This is why a multi-channel approach is essential for effective B2B lead generation. Instead of relying on one strategy to do all the heavy lifting, you create a powerful system where each channel supports the others. An email campaign can warm up leads for a follow-up call, while a targeted ad can reinforce the message from a recent webinar. This synergy not only helps you reach more people but also builds deeper relationships by meeting them where they are. Combining your outreach efforts creates a more comprehensive and resilient strategy that keeps your pipeline full, even as markets shift. It’s about creating a seamless experience that guides prospects from initial awareness to a signed deal, making every interaction count. Mix Online and Offline Strategies The most effective lead generation strategies blend digital convenience with a human touch. Online channels like SEO, content marketing, and social media are fantastic for casting a wide net and attracting initial interest. But offline tactics, such as direct mail or a well-timed phone call, can cut through the digital noise and create a memorable, personal connection. Imagine a prospect downloads your latest whitepaper (online). A few days later, they receive a call from a real person to discuss their challenges and answer their questions (offline). This combination shows you’re attentive and transforms a passive lead into an engaged prospect. By integrating both online and offline strategies, you create a comprehensive marketing strategy that meets leads at different stages of their journey. Create a Cohesive Brand Experience Consistency is key to building trust. Whether a prospect finds you through a LinkedIn post, reads an article on your blog, or gets an email from your team, the experience should feel connected and familiar. A cohesive brand experience means your messaging, tone of voice, and visual identity are consistent across every single channel. This doesn't mean saying the exact same thing everywhere, but ensuring your core message and brand personality shine through in a way that’s appropriate for each platform. This consistency helps build brand recognition and makes your company appear more professional and reliable, which is crucial when asking another business to invest in your solution. When every touchpoint reinforces your brand, you stay top-of-mind. Run Effective A/B Tests The best way to improve your outreach is to let your data guide you. A/B testing, or split testing, is a straightforward method for comparing two versions of something to see which one performs better. Don't just test your landing page headlines; apply this to all your lead generation efforts. You can test different email subject lines, call-to-action buttons, ad copy, or even the opening lines of a call script. By systematically testing these elements, you can refine your approach based on how your audience actually behaves, not on what you think will work. This iterative process of testing and optimizing is what separates good lead generation from great lead generation, helping you make small changes that deliver significant results over time. What's Next in B2B Lead Generation? Staying current with lead generation trends helps you connect with prospects in ways that feel relevant and respectful of their time. While the fundamentals of building relationships remain the same, the tools and tactics we use are always evolving. Keeping an eye on what’s next allows you to refine your strategy, ensuring your efforts continue to deliver results. Here are a few key trends that are shaping the future of B2B lead generation. Account-Based Marketing (ABM) Instead of casting a wide net, Account-Based Marketing (ABM) focuses your sales and marketing resources on a select group of high-value target accounts. Think of it as a VIP approach. It’s a highly focused business strategy where you treat an individual company as its own market, tailoring all your messaging and outreach specifically to its challenges and needs. This personalized approach builds stronger relationships from the start and often leads to higher engagement and conversion rates because your prospects feel truly seen and understood. It’s a shift from volume to value, prioritizing deep engagement with the accounts that matter most to your business. AI and Machine Learning Applications Artificial intelligence is becoming a powerful ally for B2B marketing teams. Far from being just a buzzword, AI offers practical tools to make your lead generation smarter and more efficient. For example, AI can analyze data to predict which leads are most likely to convert, allowing your team to focus its energy where it counts. A recent study shows that most B2B marketers see AI having a positive impact on B2B marketing, especially in personalizing content at scale. By handling data analysis and pattern recognition, AI frees up your team to concentrate on creative strategy and building genuine human connections with the right prospects. Interactive Content Strategies Getting a prospect’s attention is harder than ever, which is why more businesses are turning to interactive content. This goes beyond the standard blog post or whitepaper and includes things like quizzes, polls, calculators, and assessments. This type of interactive content does more than just capture attention; it creates a two-way conversation. As prospects engage, they provide you with valuable information about their needs, preferences, and pain points. You get the data you need to better qualify and segment your leads, and your audience gets a more engaging and personalized experience. It’s a win-win for building relationships and gathering critical insights. How to Optimize Your B2B Lead Generation Strategy Launching your lead generation strategies is a huge first step, but the work doesn’t stop there. The most successful B2B teams know that optimization is a continuous process, not a one-time task. Think of your strategy as a living thing that needs regular attention to perform at its best. By consistently analyzing your results, testing new ideas, and refining your methods, you can turn a good lead generation engine into a great one. This ongoing effort ensures you’re not just generating leads, but generating the right leads more efficiently over time. It’s about making small, smart adjustments that lead to significant long-term growth. This means looking beyond the initial setup of your campaigns and building a culture of improvement within your team. It's about asking "How can we do this better?" at every stage, from the first touchpoint to the final conversion. This mindset shift is what separates companies that simply get by from those that consistently outperform their goals and build a sustainable pipeline for the future. Continuously Test and Refine Your Approach Your initial approach is your best-educated guess, but data will always tell the real story. The key to optimization is to constantly test every part of your process. Experiment with different email subject lines, call-to-action buttons, ad copy, and landing page layouts to see what resonates with your target audience. An A/B test can give you clear, actionable insights into what works and what doesn’t. Don’t be afraid to try something new or pivot if an approach isn’t delivering. This cycle of testing, learning, and refining is what separates stagnant campaigns from those that produce consistent, high-quality results. Address Common Misconceptions One of the most persistent myths in lead generation is that success is all about volume. It’s easy to get caught up in chasing a higher number of leads, but this can be a major pitfall. A list of 1,000 unqualified leads is far less valuable than 50 highly qualified ones who are genuinely interested in your solution. Focusing only on quantity can cause you to overlook the importance of nurturing relationships and providing real value. Shift your mindset from "more leads" to "better leads" to ensure your sales team spends their time on conversations that are likely to convert. Implement a Referral Program Your happiest customers can be your most effective salespeople. A formal referral program encourages satisfied clients to spread the word about your business, turning their positive experiences into a powerful source of new leads. Leads generated through customer referrals often come with a layer of built-in trust, making them more likely to convert and shortening the sales cycle. You can offer incentives like discounts, credits, or gift cards to motivate customers to participate. It’s a low-cost, high-impact strategy that leverages your existing relationships to fuel new growth. Frequently Asked Questions This all sounds like a lot. Where should I even begin? The best place to start is by getting crystal clear on who you're trying to reach. Before you write a single blog post or launch an ad, sit down with your team and define your ideal customer profile. What industry are they in? What is their job title? What are their biggest challenges? Once you know exactly who you’re talking to, every other decision—from the content you create to the channels you use—becomes much easier and more effective. How can I tell if I'm generating quality leads and not just a lot of them? The true test of lead quality happens when your marketing leads are passed to your sales team. The most important metric to watch is your lead-to-opportunity conversion rate. This tells you what percentage of the leads marketing generates are actually accepted by sales as legitimate opportunities. If that number is high, you're on the right track. If it's low, it’s a sign that your marketing message might be attracting the wrong audience, and it's time to refine your targeting. How long does it typically take to see results from a new lead generation strategy? This really depends on the strategies you choose. You can see results from paid advertising on platforms like Google or LinkedIn almost immediately, which is great for a quick influx of leads. On the other hand, strategies like content marketing and SEO are long-term investments. It can take several months to build authority and rank in search results, but the payoff is a sustainable flow of organic leads that don't require a constant ad spend. My sales and marketing teams don't really talk to each other. What's a simple first step to get them aligned? The easiest way to start bridging that gap is to get both teams in the same room to agree on a shared vocabulary. Schedule a meeting with the sole purpose of defining what a "Marketing Qualified Lead" (MQL) and a "Sales Qualified Lead" (SQL) mean for your business. When marketing knows exactly what criteria a lead needs to meet before sales will engage, and sales understands the journey a lead has taken, you eliminate a huge amount of friction. Is it better to master one channel first or try a multi-channel approach from the start? While a multi-channel approach is the ultimate goal, trying to do everything at once can stretch your resources too thin. I recommend starting with one or two channels where you know your ideal customers spend their time. For many B2B companies, this might be a combination of creating valuable content for SEO and engaging professionally on LinkedIn. Focus on doing those few things really well. Once you have a solid, repeatable process, you can begin layering in other channels. Posted on July 29 at 11:08 AM

title: MGE Continues to Expand its Use of Agrivoltaics at Local Solar Facilities
summary: MGE continues to expand its use of solar grazing at local solar facilities and added honey bee hives to its agrivoltaics practice in 2026.
body_text: In 2024, Madison Gas and Electric (MGE) introduced grazing sheep at the Company’s 6-megawatt (MW) Tyto Solar array in Fitchburg. The sheep help control ground cover during the growing season, maintaining grass and brush in a sustainable way. The practice is an example of agrivoltaics, or dual-use solar, in which land is used for both solar generation and agriculture. MGE expanded its use of solar grazing the following year to the Company’s nearby Strix Solar facility and to the Hermsdorf Solar Fields in Madison. The introduction of solar grazing built on the Company’s commitment to providing pollinator habitat through native plantings at some of its local solar generation facilities, including Dane County Airport Solar, Hermsdorf Solar Fields, Morey Field Solar and the O’Brien Solar Fields. Pollinator habitats are shrinking. As native vegetation is replaced by roads, manicured lawns and non-native gardens, pollinators lose necessary food and nesting sites. A pollinator is a bee, butterfly or other agent that transfers pollen from one plant to another. This process enables fertilization and the production of food such as seeds, fruits and nuts. Hives for honey bees added to the mix This spring, MGE welcomed honey bees to the O'Brien Solar Fields, a 22-MW solar array in Fitchburg, Wis., and one of the Company’s initial pollinator sites. In partnership with a local beekeeper, five bee hives were set up and a colony of honey bees now resides at the solar array. The addition of hives further expands MGE’s practice of agrivoltaics. The bees collect nectar from some of the native pollinator plants at the site, contributing to the ecosystem. The bees also search for nectar elsewhere, typically traveling up to two miles from the hive to secure nectar from preferred sources.

title: What data center power design looks like from the utility side
summary: AI is reshaping data center power design and the grid. Takeaways from a recent UTC meeting on how utilities and hyperscalers can plan, build and adapt together.
body_text: Reliability is under pressure as extreme weather intensifies Extreme weather is already testing the limits of today’s grid, even before large data center loads are fully in the mix. Case in point: In early February, all four balancing authorities in the Carolinas hit all‑time winter peaks on the same day. Residential heating load spiked as a result, and system operators had to make hard decisions to keep the lights on. As hyperscale demand grows, these large new loads could make it harder to maintain reliability if they aren’t integrated carefully. Legislators and regulators are already talking about mandatory curtailment for data centers and other large industrial customers during emergencies to make sure life‑critical load remains the priority. For utilities, that means building in the ability to curtail while still honoring contracts and maintaining long‑term relationships with large customers. Hyperscalers are exploring their own power generation Another theme is the growing interest in “bring your own power” for large data centers. Faced with long timelines for new grid‑connected generation, hyperscalers are now looking at options like onsite gas turbines, distributed generation, nuclear microreactors and large‑scale backup solutions. While this could be a potential relief valve for some parts of the grid, it also brings a new set of coordination challenges. If more generation sits behind the fence, utilities will need clear visibility into how and when that capacity operates , how it interacts with the bulk system and what happens during abnormal conditions. There’s also a regulatory dimension to consider: Current rules don’t always accommodate these new models in some jurisdictions, so utilities, regulators and large customers will have to find ways to work together to keep the system stable. Speculation and screening are now part of the job Not every data center inquiry that hits a utility’s inbox is coming from a hyperscaler. Several participants describe a growing wave of speculative real estate activity. In other words, developers want to secure interconnection positions “just in case,” with no specific customer in mind. To protect existing members and customers, many cooperatives are tightening interconnection processes, requiring higher levels of financial commitment upfront and creating new rate structures to isolate the impact of large new loads. The goal is to make sure they don’t have to subsidize projects that may never materialize. How utilities can prepare for what’s next The UTC data center discussion reinforced the fact that hyperscale demand is creating a long‑term shift in how and where energy is consumed.

title: Let’s Talk Equity In Hiring!
summary: Achieving equity within school hiring processes is crucial for building strong educational communities. By adopting strategies that prioritize fairness and equal opportunities, districts can attract and retain talented educators from all backgrounds.
body_text: Achieving equity within school hiring processes is crucial for building strong educational communities. By adopting strategies that prioritize fairness and equal opportunities, districts can attract and retain talented educators from diverse backgrounds. ‍ Want to ensure equity in your hiring process? Let’s talk about it! Here are three effective ways to maximize the spirit of belonging and inclusivity within your workforce: ‍ Setting the Stage for Inclusive Hiring Developing clear and inclusive hiring policies is a critical step towards ensuring equity. These policies should clearly communicate the organization’s commitment to equal opportunity, while also outlining the steps involved in the selection process. Consider these four practices: ‍ Craft inclusive job descriptions that use gender-neutral language and focus on essential qualifications and skills, avoiding unnecessary requirements that may create barriers for underrepresented candidates. Reach candidates from diverse backgrounds by utilizing a variety of recruitment channels, engaging with community organizations, and leveraging professional networks. Standardize evaluation criteria to ensure consistent assessment of all candidates, based on qualifications relevant to the position. Provide bias awareness training to hiring committees to recognize and mitigate unconscious biases that may influence decision-making, ensuring a fair and unbiased evaluation process. ‍ Clear and inclusive hiring policies create a foundation for equitable recruitment and foster an environment that welcomes candidates from all backgrounds. ‍ Implementing Structured Interview Processes Structured interviews play a vital role in promoting equity by minimizing bias and subjectivity in candidate evaluation. These interviews utilize predetermined questions and evaluation criteria, ensuring a consistent assessment of all applicants. Structured interviews and assessment practices emphasize the importance of consistency and impartiality . ‍ To implement structured interviews effectively, try these Nimble-Can-Dos: ‍ Prepare standardized interview questions that directly assess the qualifications and skills required for the position. Asking the same questions to all candidates ensures fairness. Nimble’s question bank provides users with research-based questions to effectively measure the education philosophies and efficacy of educators. ‍ Use evaluation rubrics that outline the key criteria for assessing candidates' responses, promoting objective evaluation and comparison. Nimble’s Scorecard feature allows admin to standardize interview rubrics across departments and school sites with customizable rubrics. ‍ Require interviewers to document their feedback using the established evaluation rubrics, promoting transparency and accountability. Want to share a rubric with a non-Nimble user? Use the scorecard sharing functionality to ensure all interviewers have access to submit their structured interview feedback. ‍ Implementing structured interview processes has been shown to reduce bias, promote objectivity, and attract a diverse pool of qualified candidates. ‍ Consider Representation in Interview Committees: Prioritizing diverse interview committees is essential for equity in the hiring process. A diverse committee brings varied perspectives and experiences , contributing to fair decision-making. ‍ To prioritize diverse interview committees: Aim for interview committees that include individuals from diverse backgrounds, experiences, roles, and perspectives, ensuring representation. Foster an environment where committee members feel comfortable expressing diverse viewpoints, challenging assumptions, and engaging in constructive discussions. Regularly assess the committee's effectiveness, gather feedback from committee members and candidates, and make necessary adjustments to promote equity and inclusion. ‍ Prioritizing diverse perspectives in interview committees ensures a range of views are considered, leading to more equitable hiring decisions. ‍ Promoting equity within school hiring processes is essential for building inclusive educational environments. By establishing clear and inclusive hiring policies, implementing structured interviews, prioritizing representation in selection committees, schools can ensure fairness and create stronger educational communities where every individual has equal opportunities to thrive. ‍

title: Cube Semantic Layer: Deep Dive Into the Agentic Analytics Pioneer
summary: Cube nails the Meaning layer but leaves the Trust layer to you. Learn what it does well, and the upfront modeling work it asks of you.
body_text: Disclosure: This article is published by Upsolve AI. Where our product is mentioned alongside competitors, we aim to provide balanced coverage based on publicly available information. We encourage readers to evaluate all options independently. The Cube semantic layer is a universal, code-first modeling layer that defines your metrics, dimensions, joins, and access rules once, then serves them consistently to every downstream tool: BI dashboards, embedded analytics, spreadsheets, and, increasingly, AI agents. If you lead an analytics engineering team and you are trying to figure out how to feed reliable context to an analytics agent, Cube is one of the most mature options on the market. In 2026 the company has repositioned itself squarely around that use case, describing itself as an agentic analytics platform built on a semantic layer. This is a genuine deep dive, not a hype piece. We will look at how the Cube semantic layer actually works, what its D3 agentic product does, where it is strong, and where it leaves gaps that an analytics engineering lead needs to plan around. Cube deserves real credit for seeing the semantic layer as the foundation for AI agents years before it was fashionable. It also has real limitations, and the honest read is that Cube solves one layer of the context problem very well while asking a lot of upfront modeling work in return. Key Takeaways Treating the semantic layer as the foundation for AI agents is the right instinct: An agent pointed at raw tables does not know what your business means, so grounding it in governed definitions is what makes answers trustworthy rather than merely plausible. Cube saw this early. D3 is a genuine agentic platform, not a chatbot bolted onto a dashboard: Cube's agents query the semantic layer instead of the warehouse directly, so every answer traces back to definitions your team owns and can audit. Cube's real strength is the Meaning layer: Defining a metric once, enforcing it everywhere, and applying governance before a query ever runs is where Cube is genuinely excellent, and where it earns its pioneer reputation. Its limits are the Trust layer and the modeling it assumes upfront: Cube does not natively close the loop on verified answers and continuous correction, and it expects a well-authored semantic model before agents become reliable. For your evaluation, that assumption shapes your timeline more than any single feature. What Is the Cube Semantic Layer? The Cube semantic layer is a governed abstraction that sits between your data sources and everything that consumes data. Instead of every dashboard, report, and query re-deriving what "revenue" or "active customer" means, you define those concepts once in Cube. Every downstream tool then inherits the same definition and calculation logic. As Alcon's global head of data science put it in a customer story, without a shared model analysts might write twenty different queries for one core metric; with Cube, that metric is defined once and reused everywhere. Cube calls this a universal semantic layer because it is designed to serve any consumer: business intelligence tools like Tableau, Power BI, and Looker; spreadsheets; embedded analytics inside a product; and AI agents. The model itself is authored in code, using YAML, JavaScript, or Python, which lets data teams apply software engineering practices such as version control, testing, and CI/CD to their metric definitions. Where Cube Came From Cube did not start as an AI product. Founders Artyom Keydunov and Pavel Tiunov built the first version around 2019, and the open-source project took off quickly on HackerNews, crossing 10,000 GitHub stars within months. The commercial product, Cube Cloud, followed. In June 2024 the company raised a $25 million round led by Databricks Ventures , bringing its cumulative funding to $48 million across three rounds. By that point Cube reported being installed on 90,000 servers with 4.9 million users , including roughly 20% of the Fortune 1000. That history matters for an evaluation. Cube has spent years on the unglamorous, hard problems of semantic modeling: schema mapping, join logic, pre-aggregations, caching, and governance. When LLMs arrived, Cube already had the foundation that AI agents turned out to need. How Cube Became an Agentic Analytics Pioneer Cube's central argument is one that Upsolve agrees with completely: an LLM pointed at raw tables does not know what your business means. A table named orders does not tell a model whether revenue is gross or net, whether it includes tax, or whether it is recognized at order time or ship time. Cube frames the semantic layer as the missing layer of understanding that closes this gap, and that framing is correct. In June 2025 Cube shipped D3 (short for "data in cube"), which it describes as the first agentic analytics platform built on a universal semantic layer . Rather than bolting a chatbot onto a dashboard tool, D3 was designed agent-native from the start. The agents query the semantic layer, not the warehouse directly, which means every answer traces back to governed definitions instead of being improvised from raw schema. This positioning has earned Cube recognition in the 2026 Gartner Market Guide for Agentic Analytics and a growing roster of named customers, including Brex, Webflow, and Drata. For a category that barely existed two years ago, that is a real head start. Semantic SQL: The Query Language for the Layer One of Cube's more thoughtful design decisions is what it calls Semantic SQL. The team's reasoning is that AI needs a query language for the semantic layer, not just access to metric definitions. Feeding an agent a list of definitions and hoping it writes correct SQL is where accuracy breaks down. Instead, D3 agents query semantic objects directly and can create ad-hoc dimensions and measures on the fly, while a compiler translates the request into optimized, governed SQL. This is a meaningful distinction from pure text-to-SQL and where its accuracy tends to break down . The compiler, not the model, owns the final query, which sharply reduces the risk of a subtly wrong join or an unauthorized column appearing in results. Inside the Cube AI API and D3 Agents. For teams searching for the cube ai api, here is what actually sits under the hood. Cube exposes an Analytics Chat API that is agent-to-agent capable via the Model Context Protocol and integrates natively with Anthropic's Claude models, with support for bring-your-own-LLM configurations. Underneath, Cube has described building a retrieval augmented generation architecture on top of the semantic layer to surface the most relevant context to the model. D3 itself ships a small suite of purpose-built agents. Understanding what each one does helps clarify who Cube is really built for. The Semantic Model Agent This agent helps data teams build and extend the semantic model itself. It proposes and edits cubes, views, measures, and dimensions, and can automate YAML generation from cloud data sources. This is aimed at the analytics engineer, not the business user. The Workbook Agent The Workbook Agent assembles reports and visualizations inside Cube's Workbooks surface. It sits alongside point-and-click, SQL, and Python paths, so an analyst can move between manual and AI-assisted building without leaving the workflow. The Analytics Chat Agent This is the natural-language entry point for business users. It answers questions in plain language, runs multiple queries against the semantic layer, and summarizes the result. Cube also groups these capabilities as an AI Data Analyst (for data consumers) and an AI Data Engineer (for automating model development). Where Cube Excels Let's talk about the strengths, because they are substantial. Cube earned its pioneer status. Governance enforced at query-compile time: Because row-level and role-based rules are applied before SQL is emitted , an agent acting for one tenant cannot construct a query that returns another tenant's rows. The security boundary is the compiler, which the agent does not control. This makes governed agents genuinely safe to put in front of external customers. True multi-surface delivery: The same model feeds BI tools, spreadsheets, embedded apps, and external agents over MCP. Define once, deliver anywhere is not marketing here; it is the architecture. Open-source flexibility: Cube Core is open source, which reduces lock-in and gives engineering teams full control. This is a real advantage for teams that want to own their infrastructure. Metric consistency at scale: When your AI assistant, your dashboards, and your embedded product all read from the same model, the numbers reconcile. For a data team tired of arguing about whose revenue figure is right, this is the whole point. For an analytics engineering lead who already values governance and code-first workflows, Cube feels like it was built by people who share your priorities. To go deeper on the foundational concepts, our guide to semantic layer fundamentals covers why this abstraction matters regardless of which vendor you choose. How Cube Handles the Metrics Layer Cube's metrics handling is one of its most refined areas. Metrics are first-class objects: you define a measure once, attach its calculation logic and access rules, and every consumer inherits it. This is what keeps a KPI consistent whether it appears in a board deck, a customer-facing dashboard, or an agent's chat reply. That said, the metrics layer and the semantic layer are related but not identical concepts, and the distinction affects how you evaluate any tool in this space. If you want to understand exactly how metric definitions differ from the broader model and why that matters for agent accuracy, see our breakdown of Cube's approach to the metrics layer and where the two ideas overlap. The Three-Layer Lens: Where Cube Fits Here is where an honest evaluation gets specific. Every analytics agent needs three layers of context to produce trustworthy answers, and mapping any tool against those layers is the clearest way to see what it does and does not cover. Structure is what data exists: schemas, tables, lineage, relationships, and usage patterns. Meaning is what the data means at your company: metrics, KPIs, business rules, definitions, and tribal knowledge. Trust is which answers have been validated: verified answers, golden assets, usage signals, and corrections that compound over time. Cube is excellent at the Meaning layer. That is its heritage and its core strength. It also touches Structure, since the model encodes relationships and joins. What Cube does not natively provide is the Trust layer: a systematic loop that verifies which specific answers can be trusted , promotes them to golden assets, learns from real user conversations, and detects when context has drifted or gone stale. This is not a knock on Cube's engineering. It is a difference in scope. Cube was designed as a semantic layer first, and the Trust layer is a distinct problem that requires its own workflow: evaluation suites, golden query testing, and human-in-the-loop refinement based on how business users actually interact with the agent. For a full treatment of how all three layers fit together, see where Cube fits in the three-layer architecture and why solving one layer is not the same as solving all three. The Upfront Modeling Question The second consideration is practical rather than architectural: Cube expects you to bring or build a semantic model. The Semantic Model Agent can accelerate this, and automating YAML generation from cloud sources is a genuine help. But the underlying assumption remains that a hand-authored, well-maintained model is the starting point. For teams that already run a disciplined semantic layer, this is a feature, not a cost. Your investment pays off immediately. For the many organizations that do not have a well-maintained model, or whose dbt YAML was last meaningfully updated years ago, the upfront modeling work becomes the project before the project. You cannot get value from the agent until the model is in good shape. This is worth naming plainly because it shapes your timeline. If your data team's reality is a sprawl of undocumented tables and definitions that live in people's heads and Slack threads, the honest question is not "which agent is smartest" but "how much modeling work stands between us and a reliable answer." This is where design philosophy matters more than any feature list. Some platforms, including Upsolve, are built to start encoding context without a complete pre-existing semantic model, and to treat the Trust layer (verified answers and continuous correction) as part of the core workflow rather than something you bolt on later. For a team without a mature model, that can be the deciding factor. It is not a knock on Cube; it is a reason to make context coverage and modeling burden explicit criteria before you commit. Cube vs. What to Look For: An Evaluation Snapshot If you are comparing Cube against other approaches, it helps to score any option against the capabilities that actually determine agent reliability rather than against feature checklists. Capability 📄 What to Check Where Cube Lands Structure (schema, lineage) Does it model relationships and joins? Strong Meaning (metrics, rules) Are definitions governed and reused everywhere? Very strong Trust (verified answers) Is there a loop for golden assets and validation? Not native Upfront modeling required Can you start without a complete model? Significant model expected Governance Enforced before query execution? Strong, compile-time Deployment surfaces BI, embedded, chat, external agents? Broad, multi-surface Open source Can you self-host the core? Yes, Cube Core The pattern here is consistent: Cube is a top-tier answer for the Meaning layer and governance, and it is genuinely open. The areas to plan around are the Trust layer and the modeling investment. Neither is a dealbreaker, but both decide how much work stands between you and a reliable agent, so surface them early rather than after a build stalls. When you reach the platform-selection stage, our guide to evaluating analytics agent builder platforms lays out the full evaluation criteria for analytics-specific agent builders. What a Cube Evaluation Should Pressure-Test The strongest evaluations do not ask whether Cube is good, because it is. They ask where it fits your team's reality and where you will have to fill gaps yourself. Three points are worth stress-testing before you commit. A Semantic Layer Alone Does Not Guarantee Accuracy A semantic layer is necessary for reliable agents, but it is not sufficient on its own. The Meaning layer answers "what does this metric mean," yet it does not answer "has this specific answer been verified and trusted." It is tempting to assume that once definitions are governed, accuracy is solved, but in practice accuracy also depends on validation and continuous correction. As a16z argued in its analysis, data agents are essentially useless without the right context , and context is broader than definitions alone. Evaluate all three layers, not just the one a given tool leads with. The Modeling Effort Is Easy to Underestimate Because D3 demos are impressive, it is easy to assume the path to production is short. The demo runs on a clean, well-authored model, and your production reality may not. Before committing, audit the honest state of your existing model and budget for the modeling work Cube expects. That work, rather than the agent's intelligence, is usually what determines your time to value. Accuracy Drifts Without a Trust and Refinement Loop An agent that is accurate on day one can drift as data, definitions, and business rules change. Without a loop that captures corrections and promotes verified answers, quality erodes quietly and no one notices until a stakeholder does. Ask specifically how a platform handles verified answers, golden query testing, and improvement from real user conversations, and plan to build that layer yourself if the tool does not provide it. Where the Cube Semantic Layer Fits, and Where It Does Not Cube earned its reputation as an agentic analytics pioneer. It saw the semantic layer as the foundation for AI agents early, built a mature open-source core, and shipped a thoughtful agent-native product in D3. For analytics engineering leads who value governance, open source, and code-first workflows, and who already maintain a disciplined semantic model, Cube is a serious and credible option. The two things to plan around are the Trust layer, which Cube does not natively close, and the upfront modeling investment it expects. Neither should disqualify Cube. But if your team does not already run a disciplined semantic model, or if verified and self-correcting answers are non-negotiable, weigh those requirements deliberately and compare how each platform, Cube included, covers all three layers rather than one. If you are further along and comparing platforms head to head, the clearest next step is to evaluate every option against the three layers of context that determine whether an agent actually works in production. See how agent platforms compare to Cube for a structured way to run that comparison across governance, context coverage, and production readiness. Frequently Asked Questions What is the Cube semantic layer? The Cube semantic layer is a universal, code-first modeling layer that defines metrics, dimensions, joins, and access rules once and serves them consistently to BI tools, embedded analytics, spreadsheets, and AI agents. It acts as a single source of truth so every downstream tool uses the same definitions. Is Cube open source? Yes. Cube's core, known as Cube Core, is open source and has grown to roughly 17,000 GitHub stars. Cube also offers a commercial product, Cube Cloud, which adds managed hosting, governance features, and the D3 agentic analytics platform. What is Cube D3? Cube D3 (short for "data in cube") is Cube's agentic analytics platform, launched in June 2025. It layers AI agents directly on the semantic layer so that answers stay grounded in governed definitions rather than being improvised from raw database schema. Does the Cube AI API support natural language and MCP? Yes. Cube's Analytics Chat API is agent-to-agent capable via the Model Context Protocol and integrates natively with Claude models, with support for bringing your own LLM. Underneath, Cube uses a retrieval augmented generation architecture on top of the semantic layer. Do I need an existing semantic model to use Cube? Cube is designed around a hand-authored semantic model. Its Semantic Model Agent can automate parts of model creation, but the platform generally expects a well-maintained model as the starting point. Teams without one should budget for the upfront modeling work before agents become reliable. Where does Cube fall short for analytics agents? Cube is strong at the Meaning layer (governed metrics and definitions) but does not natively provide the Trust layer: a systematic loop for verified answers, golden assets, and continuous accuracy improvement from real user conversations. It also requires significant upfront semantic modeling, which can slow time to value for teams without an existing model.

Total assets for the Company at June 30, 2026, were $1.17 billion, a decrease of $114.8 million from year end 2025, but $6.2 million or 0.53% higher compared to $1.17 billion as of June 30, 2025. The year-to-date change primarily reflects annual maturities of municipal non arbitrage relationships and lower cash balances used to pay off two maturing advances totaling $25.0 million, as well as a cyclical decrease in deposit balances. Contributing to the Company's year-over-year growth in assets was growth in the Company's gross loan portfolio of $28.8 million, or 3.06%, compared to the 2025 period. Deposit balances increased $48.7 million, or 5.22%, compared to the same period in 2025 but decreased $89.0 million or 8.31% since year end 2025 reflecting cyclical changes. The year-over-year loan growth was primarily funded by a combination of cash, maturities of securities, as well as an increase in core deposits. The Company's securities portfolio totaled $128 million as of June 30, 2026, an 11.45% decrease compared to $144.6 million as of December 31, 2025. The portfolio is classified as available-for-sale and is required to be reported at fair market value with the unrealized loss, net of a deferred tax adjustment, as an adjustment to total equity. Such unrealized losses reflect the interest rate environment, as current rates remain below the coupon rates on the securities, resulting in a fair market value lower than current book values. As of June 30, 2026, the adjustment to equity was $9.4 million, representing an improvement of $3.1 million from the adjustment to equity of $12.5 million on June 30, 2026 and $9.6 million as of December 31, 2025. Total net interest income for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026, increased $1.4 million, or 13.68%, to $11.2 million, compared to $9.9 million for the same quarter in 2025. The quarter-over-quarter improvement reflects an increase of $1.1 million, or 7.72%, in interest and fees on loans due to strong loan growth and higher yields, partially offset by higher interest on deposits expense of $37,533, or 0.94%. Net interest income for the six months ended June 30, 2026, increased $2.9 million or 14.81%, to $22.2 million, compared to $19.3 million for the same period in 2025, reflecting the same trends. The provision for credit losses for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026, was $720,967 compared to $407,046 for the same period in 2025. The year-to-date provision for credit losses was $1.1 million, compared to $732,100 for the same period in 2025. The $380,373 year-over-year increase was driven primarily by strong loan growth. The provision for credit losses for June 30, 2026, was determined under Accounting Standard No. 2016-13, Measurement of Credit Losses on Financial Instruments, commonly referenced as the Current Expected Credit Losses, or CECL. Total non-interest income for the second quarter ended June 30, 2026, of $2.3 million increased $254,036, or 12.34%, compared to $2.1million for the same period in 2025. Total non-interest income for the six months ended June 30, 2026, grew to $4.1 million, compared to $3.6 million for the six months ended June 30, 2025, an increase of $420,767, or 11.57% year-over-year. Total non-interest expenses increased $497,838, or 7.47%, for the second quarter comparison period, and $1.1 million, or 7.98%, for the six months period year-over-year. Equity capital increased to $120.9 million, with a book value per share of $21.58, as of June 30, 2026, compared to equity capital of $113.7 million and a book value per share of $20.36 as of December 31, 2025, and $106.3 million and book value per share of $18.69 as of June 30, 2025. This change includes a decrease of $237,432 in unrealized losses in the investment portfolio year-to-date and a decrease of $3.1 million year-over-year, due to changing bond rates, which increased the fair market value of the investment portfolio, as well as an increase of $6.3 million year-to-date and an increase of $12.8 million year-over-year in retained earnings. The unrealized loss position is considered temporary and does not impact the Company's regulatory capital ratios. In the fourth quarter of 2025, the Company completed the optional redemption of all fifteen of the Company's outstanding shares of its Series A Fixed-to-Floating Rate Non-Cumulative Perpetual Preferred Stock. The preferred stock value of $1,500,000 was included in the Company's equity capital as of June 30, 2025. President and CEO Christopher Caldwell commented on the Company's results: "Through the first half of 2026, the company continued its strong performance. Community banking thrives through relationship-based banking and this long-term approach to clients and our communities continues to serve us well. Our inclusion in both the ABA Nasdaq Community Bank Index and the Russell 2000 Index has increased the Company's visibility among investors and may support broader market awareness of our stock over time. Tangible book value per share increased by 17% for the year-to-date period compared to the same period of 2025. Year-to-date earnings per share increased 20% compared to the same period last year, and 16% for the second quarter compared to the same quarter of 2025. These results demonstrate the Company's commitment to serving our customers as Vermont's Community Bank. We are grateful for the trust that our communities, clients, and shareholders have placed in us." As previously announced, the Company declared a quarterly cash dividend of $0.25 per share payable August 1, 2026, to shareholders of record as of July 15, 2026. About Community Bancorp. Community Bancorp. is the parent holding company for Community National Bank, headquartered in Derby, Vermont. Community National Bank is an independent bank that has been serving its communities since 1851, with retail banking offices located in Derby, Derby Line, Island Pond, Barton, Newport, Troy, St. Johnsbury, Montpelier, Barre, Lyndonville, Morrisville and Enosburg Falls as well as loan offices located in Burlington, Vermont and Lebanon, New Hampshire Forward Looking Statements This press release contains forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995, as amended, including, without limitation, statements about the Company's financial condition, capital status, dividend payment practices, business outlook and affairs. title: Behavioral Health
summary: Behavioral health, including mental health, is a key driver of whole health. We take a holistic approach to behavioral health needs.
body_text: Related Research Research Acupuncture Found to Reduce Opioid Use and Emergency Department Visits In response to the need for pain relief therapies that don’t involve opioid medications, acupuncture is one recommended alternative in addition to cognitive behavioral therapy, physical therapy, and non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs). The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid services (CMS) announced in January 2020 that it would cover acupuncture for chronic low back pain in Medicare beneficiaries, citing the potential for acupuncture to reduce overuse of and addiction to opioids. Although acupuncture has been proposed to reduce exposure to opioids, few studies have examined its effect on lowering prescribed opioid use because is very difficult to study due to variations in applied techniques and a strong potential for placebo effects. This study compared outcomes in people who used acupuncture to those who used non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) and and/or physical therapy (PT). Health Equity Whole Health And What Drives It June 2022 What's Driving Our Health Seeing health more broadly is key to improving it. We conducted a nationally representative survey of adults to establish benchmarks and guide efforts. February 2024 Research Low Back Pain Treatment Moving from Low Value Services to Holistic Solutions As one of the most common and disabling conditions among adults, low back pain can be treated in numerous ways. However, many treatments have proven ineffective and potentially harmful. Published guidelines have been updated to avoid low-value services like overuse of diagnostic imaging, opioids, spinal injections, and surgery. Researchers examined trends over nine years to see how quickly providers were moving away from these low-value services. Understanding treatment trends is helpful when designing holistic programs for low back pain. Health Equity Whole Health And What Drives It June 2022
