title: Collections Strategy for Solo Dental Practices
body_text: Solo dental practice collections is the end-to-end process a solo dentist uses to collect revenue from insurance payers and patients — starting from pre-visit insurance verification, through claim submission and denial management, to 90-day accounts receivable recovery. Best-in-class solo practices collect 98%+ of adjusted net production , maintain AR under 30 days, and resubmit every denied claim. Most solo practices fall short: the industry average collection rate is 91–95% , leaving $40,000–$80,000 on the table annually for a $1 million practice. Running a solo dental practice means wearing every hat — clinician, business owner, and billing manager — all at once. When you're chair-side treating patients back-to-back, insurance follow-up falls behind, patient balances go uncollected, and your accounts receivable quietly grows. A practice collecting 93% instead of 98% leaves $45,000 uncollected on $900,000 in annual production — preventable revenue loss driven by the same billing gaps that compound across every pay period. This guide gives you a complete solo dental practice collections system. It covers benchmarks to measure against, a step-by-step process from pre-visit to 90-day AR recovery, and practical guidance on when to keep billing in-house versus outsource. We also cover how AI tools reduce the upstream collection burden before claims are filed. Your front desk can focus on revenue recovery instead of call volume. For the full revenue cycle context, see our dental revenue cycle management guide for solo practices. A healthy solo dental practice collects 98%+ of adjusted net production , keeps AR under 30 days, and resubmits every denied claim. The biggest revenue leaks — skipped pre-visit verification, delayed claim submission, and patient balances left uncollected at checkout — are process failures, not staffing failures. This guide gives you the benchmarks, the 90-day follow-up calendar, and the upstream tools to close those gaps without adding headcount. Key Takeaways Revenue benchmarks: Target 98% or higher — A healthy solo dental practice net collection rate is 98%+ of adjusted production. Practices consistently below 95% have a systemic billing problem. Uncollected revenue compounds fast — A 5% collection gap on an $800,000 practice means $40,000 in preventable annual revenue loss — roughly 150–200 new patient appointments worth of production, never collected. Rework every denied claim — According to Beckers Healthcare , 65% of denied claims are never worked or resubmitted — that's permanent revenue loss. Collect before the patient leaves the chair — Collection success drops ~20% the moment a patient walks out without paying. The highest-leverage billing moment is before they stand up. Operations and staffing: Keep CDT codes current — The 2026 CDT code updates brought 31 new CDT codes among 60 total changes. Outdated codes cause denials; staying current is direct revenue protection. Key person risk stops cash flow — Most solo dental offices have one person who knows the billing system. When they're out, collections pause. Reduce that dependency before it becomes a cash flow crisis. AI receptionists create front desk bandwidth — When Arini captures insurance details during the scheduling call and handles call volume 24/7, your team can focus on AR follow-up and claim appeals instead of answering the phone. How We Evaluated Solo Dental Practice Collection Benchmarks Based on our analysis of industry billing data, published dental practice benchmarks from ADA, MGMA, and dental billing associations, and interviews with solo dental practice owners, we evaluated solo dental practice collections systems across six criteria: net collection rate, AR days, clean claim rate, aged AR percentages, denial management, and upstream billing integration. The benchmarks in this guide reflect what consistently high-performing solo dental practices achieve — not the industry average, but the attainable standard. Industry averages tell you what's typical. Best-in-class tells you what's possible without adding headcount. What Is a Good Solo Dental Practice Collection Rate? A healthy solo dental practice collections rate is 98% or higher of adjusted net production ( per industry benchmarks ), with accounts receivable under 30 days and less than 5% of total AR aged beyond 90 days. Practices consistently below 95% have a systemic billing problem — not a bad month. According to dental billing benchmarks , the industry average falls between 91–95% — meaning the typical practice is already leaving revenue on the table. Here's what each tier looks like in practice: Comparison Table Metric Industry Benchmark Red Flag Threshold Best-in-Class Net Collection Rate 98%+ of adjusted production Below 95% 98–100% AR Days Under 30 days Above 45 days 25 days or fewer Clean Claim Rate 95%+ on first submission Below 90% 97%+ AR Over 90 Days Less than 5% of total AR Above 10% Under 3% AR Over 60 Days Less than 15% of total AR Above 20% Under 10% Source: Dental billing KPI benchmarks The Dollar Impact of Every Percentage Point The dollar impact is concrete. On a practice billing $800,000 annually, a 5% collection gap costs $40,000 per year — revenue already earned but never collected. Improving from 93% to 98% on a $1 million practice adds approximately $50,000 in annual revenue. That's equivalent to 200–250 new patient appointments without acquiring a single new patient. Solo practices run 62–68% overhead versus 58–60% for group practices. That overhead disadvantage means every uncollected dollar hurts proportionally more. For a complete breakdown, see industry dental overhead benchmarks . The AR Ratio Rule Total AR should equal no more than 1.0× your average monthly production. If your AR balance is growing faster than your production, your collections system has a structural gap — not a staffing problem. This is a reliable early-warning indicator solo dentists can track. The 3 Front-End Collections Mistakes Solo Dentists Make Solo dental practices are uniquely vulnerable to billing breakdowns. One person — often the only front desk employee — carries the entire billing operation alongside scheduling, patient communication, and everything else. These three mistakes happen before the claim is ever filed. Skipping pre-visit insurance verification — Eligibility errors cause up to 35% of denials, according to dental claim data . Verifying coverage before the appointment prevents the most avoidable claim failures. Not collecting at time of service — Collection success drops approximately 20% the moment a patient walks out without paying. The highest-leverage collection moment is before the patient leaves the chair, not after a statement cycle. Submitting claims more than 24 hours after treatment — Delayed claim submission extends your AR cycle immediately and signals disorganization to payers. Electronic submission within 24 hours is the standard for best-in-class practices. The 3 Back-End Collections Mistakes Solo Dentists Make These three mistakes happen after the claim is filed — and they compound quietly until they show up as chronic cash flow gaps. Ignoring denied claims — According to Beckers Healthcare , 65% of denied dental insurance claims are never worked or resubmitted, representing permanent revenue loss. Every denial that goes unchallenged is money the practice already earned and will never collect. Relying on one billing specialist — When that person goes on vacation, takes sick leave, or resigns, billing workflows stop. This "key person risk" causes predictable, recurring cash flow gaps in solo dental office collections. Using outdated CDT codes — January 2026 brought 31 new CDT codes among 60 total changes. Annual code training for everyone who touches claims is a direct revenue protection activity. Step 1 — Build a Pre-Visit Collections System Pre-visit insurance verification is the most effective way to prevent claim denials in solo dental practice collections. Every appointment should include a pre-visit verification sequence that catches eligibility problems, coverage limits, and documentation gaps before they become denials. Insurance Verification Checklist (48–72 Hours Out) Verify patient eligibility and active benefits with the payer directly or through your practice management software (PMS) Confirm annual maximum, remaining benefits, deductible status, and waiting periods for planned procedures Check coordination of benefits (COB) for patients with dual insurance coverage — filing in the wrong order causes immediate secondary claim denials Identify prior authorization requirements for periodontal scaling and root planing (SRP), implants, or other procedures that routinely trigger documentation requests Document all verified information in the patient's chart before the appointment date Present Financial Expectations Before the Appointment Patients who understand their financial responsibility before treatment pay more reliably. They're not surprised by a balance afterward. Pre-treatment estimates give patients a clear breakdown of what insurance covers versus their out-of-pocket responsibility. Signed financial agreements for treatment plans over $500 create documented commitment that protects you at the collections stage. Pro Tip: Automating insurance verification reduces the manual workload and catches errors your team might miss on a busy scheduling day — especially for dual-coverage patients where COB sequencing errors cause costly secondary claim rejections. Run Payer-Specific AR Tracking Calculate AR days separately for each of your major insurance carriers. If one payer consistently takes 45+ days while others resolve in 20, that's a carrier-level problem — not a global billing breakdown. Identifying the underperforming payer is the first step to fixing it. Step 2 — Submit Clean Claims Within 24 Hours Your clean claim rate is a key metric for improving cash flow in solo dental practice collections. A clean claim — submitted within 24 hours, error-free, with all supporting documentation attached — is a direct path from service delivery to payment receipt. What Makes a Claim "Clean" in 2026 Current CDT code updated for 2026 (31 new codes among 60 total changes — verify your PMS fee schedule is updated) Correct tooth numbers, surfaces, and quadrants matching the treatment notes Required X-rays, periodontal charts, or clinical narratives attached for procedures that routinely trigger documentation requests Correct primary/secondary payer sequencing for dual-insured patients Provider NPI and Tax ID matching your active credentialing on file with each payer Submission Best Practices Submit electronically — Electronic Funds Transfer (EFT) speeds insurance reimbursement versus paper checks and eliminates keying errors Confirm claim receipt within 7 days — unacknowledged claims should trigger immediate follow-up Flag any claim not acknowledged within 14 days for active payer outreach. Dental billing experts recommend proactive follow-up at day 14. Don't let claims stall in payer processing queues According to dental claim data , 15–20% of dental insurance claims are denied on first submission. Best-in-class practices achieve denial rates in the 3–6% range. The gap between 15% and 3–6% is almost entirely preventable through verification, documentation, and current coding — not by submitting more claims. Periodontal Procedures Require Extra Documentation Scaling and root planing (SRP) and other periodontal procedures experience higher-than-average denial rates. Submit with periodontal charting from the current visit, probing depths, bleeding points, and a clinical narrative. Claims submitted with complete documentation clear faster and get denied less. Step 3 — Collect Patient Balances at Time of Service Every solo dental office collections system must make point-of-service collection a non-negotiable standard. Collection rates drop significantly the instant a patient leaves without paying — and keep declining as the balance ages. At-chair collection practices — collecting what insurance doesn't cover: Collect copays and coinsurance at time of service — not at checkout, not via a statement mailed two weeks later. At the chair, before the patient gets up. Offer multiple payment methods — credit card, debit, HSA/FSA, and digital payment. The easier the payment experience, the higher the collection rate. For outstanding and future balances: Leverage text-to-pay for outstanding balances — text-to-pay for dental patient collections dramatically improves collection speed. Patients respond to a payment link on their phone far faster than to a paper statement in the mail. Use payment plans for larger treatment balances — post-insurance patient balance collection becomes significantly easier when a signed payment plan is in place before the patient leaves. A signed agreement is a commitment; an unpaid statement is a wish. For large treatment plans: Present online payment plans for dental practices before treatment begins. Document the arrangement in writing, collect a signature, and set up recurring automatic billing. In-house payment plans reduce write-offs on large balances — but only when payment terms are clearly documented and automatically charged on schedule. The ADA recommends a written financial policy for every practice. It should outline payment expectations, acceptable payment methods, and consequences of non-payment. Present it to every patient before treatment begins. Practices with a signed financial policy collect more consistently and write off less. Step 4 — Your 90-Day AR Collections Calendar No competitor covering solo dental practice collections provides a day-by-day collections action plan. Here is exactly what should happen at each stage after service is rendered: Days 0–45: Submit and confirm Comparison Table Day Action Responsible Party Day 0 — Service Day Collect copay and estimated patient out-of-pocket; consider requiring a signed financial agreement for treatments over $500 (adjust this threshold based on your practice) Front desk / treatment coordinator Day 1 Submit insurance claim electronically with all required documentation attached (X-rays, charts, narratives) Billing coordinator Day 7 Confirm claim receipt with payer; verify no missing documentation flags Billing coordinator Day 14 Follow up on any unacknowledged or pending claims — do not wait for payer to contact you Billing coordinator Day 30 Send friendly patient statement for any remaining patient balance; flag any insurance claim unpaid past 30 days for active follow-up Billing coordinator Day 45 Run AR aging report; any unpaid claim beyond 45 days triggers mandatory follow-up call to payer Billing coordinator Days 60–90+: Escalate and resolve Comparison Table Day Action Responsible Party Day 60 Send second patient statement with firmer tone; offer payment plan options; call patient directly for balances over $200 (set your threshold based on practice economics) Billing coordinator / practice owner Day 90 Send final past-due notice; internally review whether to write off, send to third-party collections, or finalize a payment plan Practice owner Day 90+ Consider third-party collections for persistent balances; write off genuinely uncollectable accounts per your written financial policy Practice owner The 90-day window is critical. AR past 90 days is notoriously difficult to recover — every dollar that ages past that threshold carries a significantly higher probability of permanent write-off. Your goal: close or resolve 95%+ of accounts before Day 90. To systematize the Day 30 and Day 60 patient statement workflow, use auto-send statements for dental practices. Automated billing tools ensure no patient balance falls through the cracks. This is especially important when your front desk is managing a busy in-office schedule. For a deeper focus on the AR aging side of this process, see our guide on how to reduce AR days in your solo practice. Managing Insurance Denials: How Solo Practices Win Appeals According to Beckers Healthcare , 65% of denied dental insurance claims are never worked or resubmitted. For a solo practice billing $900,000 annually with a 15% denial rate, that's $45,000–$90,000 every year in permanent revenue loss. Nearly two-thirds of denials going unchallenged. The fix isn't to submit fewer claims — it's to build a denial response workflow that treats every denial as an accounts receivable task, not a write-off. Every Denial Needs a Documented Response Track denials by reason code — "missing documentation" and "procedure not covered" require different remedies. Grouping denials by reason code identifies your highest-volume problem and an effective fix. Resubmit clean — correct the error, attach supporting documentation (X-rays, periodontal charts, narratives), and resubmit within the payer's appeal window Know your appeal deadlines — most payers allow 90–180 days from denial date to appeal; letting this window lapse means the revenue is permanently gone Track payer-specific denial patterns — if one carrier denies SRP claims at a disproportionately high rate, that's a documentation or pre-authorization gap, not a universal coding issue 2026 CDT Code Updates January 2026 introduced 31 new CDT codes among 60 total changes across multiple procedure categories. Annual CDT code training for every person who touches claims — including the dentist who develops treatment plans — is a direct revenue protection activity. Outdated codes cause denials. Denied claims cost revenue. Dual Coverage Coordination Errors Patients with two insurance plans create COB (Coordination of Benefits) billing complexity. Filing the secondary claim before the primary adjudicates causes immediate denials. Sequencing payers incorrectly does the same. Always confirm COB order during pre-visit verification. Document it in the patient chart. File primary first. Never submit secondary until you have the primary EOB in hand. Outsource vs. In-House vs. AI: Choosing the Right Approach For solo dental office collections, there's no universally correct answer — but there are clear signals that point toward each approach. Here's a practical comparison across the criteria that matter most: Comparison Table Criteria DIY In-House Outsourced Billing AI Automation Monthly Cost Staff salary + benefits (fixed cost) Typically 4–8% of collections (variable) Subscription-based (lower than outsourcing for most practices) AR Day Impact Varies by staff skill and available bandwidth Can improve significantly when managed by experienced billers Improves through automated workflows, fewer data entry errors Error Rate Dependent on individual staff training and workload Lower with experienced billers using dedicated systems Reduced through automated claim scrubbing and eligibility checks Staff Bandwidth Consumed entirely by billing and administrative tasks Frees in-house staff for patient-facing work Frees front desk from call volume, creating focused billing time Best For Practices with experienced billing staff and denial rates under 10% Practices with AR90+ above 10%, denial rates above 15%, or no dedicated billing staff Practices wanting in-house control with automation for verification, reminders, and patient communication Outsourcing Trigger Signals Consider outsourcing if your AR days consistently exceed 45, your denial rate is above 15%, your AR90+ balance is above 10% of total AR, or you have no dedicated billing staff at all. External billing companies bring specialist knowledge and established payer relationships — but they add cost and communication friction between your practice and the people managing your revenue. The Key Person Risk Problem Most solo dental practices have one individual holding the majority of billing knowledge — codes, payer contacts, where files are saved, and how your PMS is configured. When that person takes vacation, falls ill, or resigns, billing workflows slow or stop entirely. This key person dependency causes predictable, recurring cash flow gaps that compound over time. AI automation reduces key person dependency for routine, repeatable tasks — eligibility verification, statement dispatch, payment reminders, and patient communication — while keeping claims knowledge inside the practice. For more on how automating billing inquiries in dental practices reduces per-transaction workload, see our detailed breakdown. For most solo practices with capable billing staff, a hybrid approach works best. Handle daily claims in-house. Use AI tools to automate verification, reminders, and patient communication. Outsource only when your metrics consistently hit the trigger thresholds above. How Does an AI Receptionist Reduce the Collections Burden? Arini is the leading AI receptionist for solo dental practice collections — capturing insurance details at the scheduling call before the billing burden even begins. The most overlooked insight in solo dental practice collections strategy: the billing problem often starts at the phone. When a patient calls to schedule, your front desk has an opportunity to capture insurance information, verify eligibility, and set financial expectations — before the appointment date. When that call goes to voicemail or gets rushed, the upstream billing work doesn't happen, and the downstream collections burden grows. How Arini's AI receptionist reduces collections burden before claims are filed: Upstream data capture: Insurance capture on the call — Arini collects patient insurance details during the scheduling call, even after hours, even when your front desk is occupied with in-office patients. That information flows directly to your practice management software (PMS), reducing the eligibility verification workload on your billing team before the appointment day. Deep PMS integration reduces data entry errors — Arini integrates directly with your practice management software — including OpenDental, EagleSoft, Denticon, CareStack, Cloud9, Curve Dental, Dentrix, DentrixAscend, SoftDent, and PracticeWeb. Patient data flows to the PMS without manual re-entry. Manual re-entry errors are a leading source of claim rejections. Front desk bandwidth: 24/7 availability creates uninterrupted billing time — When Arini handles incoming patient calls around the clock, your front desk isn't pulled off AR follow-up tasks to answer the phone. That uninterrupted time translates directly into faster claim submission, more consistent follow-up on the 90-day calendar, and better denial response. 300ms response latency — Calls are handled instantly. No hold time frustrates patients calling about billing questions or appointment balances. Patients who get immediate, helpful responses pay more promptly. HIPAA compliant — All patient data captured during scheduling calls is encrypted and protected under role-based access controls, meeting HIPAA requirements for protected health information. Patients interact naturally without knowing they're speaking with AI. Revenue impact: Increase revenue without increasing headcount — By handling call volume that would otherwise require additional staff, Arini gives solo dental practices the functional bandwidth of a larger team without the fixed overhead cost. Real results from dental practices using Arini: Unified Dental Care achieved a 12% increase in revenue after adopting Arini's AI receptionist Kare Mobile generated $56,000 in new patient appointments in their first month Normandy Lake achieved a 90% call answer rate — ensuring no patient inquiry, including billing questions, went unanswered For practices managing patient payment outreach, recovering patient revenue with AI outreach covers the follow-up workflow in detail. Collections Metrics Every Solo Dentist Should Track Monthly Running solo dental practice collections without a monthly metrics review is like treating a patient without reviewing their chart first. These five numbers tell you whether your billing system is working — or quietly losing revenue you've already earned. Benchmark Metrics Table Metric Industry Benchmark Red Flag Threshold Best-in-Class Net Collection Rate 98%+ of adjusted production Below 95% 98–100% AR Days Under 30 days Above 45 days 25 days or fewer Clean Claim Rate 95%+ on first submission Below 90% 97%+ AR Over 90 Days Less than 5% of total AR Above 10% Under 3% AR Over 60 Days Less than 15% of total AR Above 20% Under 10% Sources: Dental billing KPI benchmarks , AR benchmarks How to Run Your Monthly Metrics Review Pull an AR aging report from your PMS — bucket by 0–30, 31–60, 61–90, and 90+ days Calculate your net collection rate : total collections ÷ adjusted net production (gross production minus contractual write-offs and insurance adjustments) Calculate your clean claim rate : total claims paid on first submission ÷ total claims submitted in the period Compare each metric to the benchmarks above and flag any red-flag thresholds for immediate investigation Run payer-specific AR analysis : calculate AR days separately for each of your major insurance carriers — identify which payers are underperforming and escalate accordingly One Benchmark to Prioritize Your AR total should be 1.0× or less of one month's average production. If your AR balance is growing while production stays flat, the gap is collections — not patient volume. This single number gives you an early warning before problems compound. For a complete 2026 benchmark breakdown, including how solo dental practices compare to group practices and DSOs, see our dental net collection rate benchmarks for 2026. Final Verdict There is no single approach that works for every solo dental practice. Here is how to match your situation to the right strategy. If your metrics are in range: For practices with experienced in-house billing and denial rates under 10% , the highest-ROI move is tightening upstream systems — pre-visit verification, 24-hour claim submission, and a consistent 90-day follow-up calendar — without adding headcount or outsourcing. If your metrics are in the red: For practices with AR days consistently above 45 or denial rates above 15% , outsourced billing brings specialist expertise and established payer relationships that often close the gap faster than internal process changes alone. If call volume is the bottleneck: For practices where front desk call volume is the bottleneck — where incoming calls interrupt AR follow-up, claim appeals, and payment posting — the upstream fix is the most direct path to better collections. Arini's AI receptionist handles patient calls 24/7 and captures insurance details at scheduling. Your team gets uninterrupted time for the billing work that actually recovers revenue. For most solo dental practices, the right answer is a hybrid: handle daily claims in-house while using AI tools to automate verification, patient reminders, and call handling — freeing your team to focus on denial follow-up and AR recovery instead of answering the phone. Book a Demo — see how capturing insurance details at the scheduling call reduces eligibility denials from day one. Frequently Asked Questions What is a dental collection rate? A dental collection rate is the percentage of revenue a practice collects relative to its adjusted net production — gross production minus contractual write-offs and insurance adjustments. For example, a practice that produces $1,000,000 in adjusted production and collects $980,000 has a 98% collection rate. The industry benchmark is 98% or higher ; practices below 95% are consistently losing revenue to preventable billing gaps. How do I improve collections in my dental practice? To improve collections in a solo dental practice, focus on three high-leverage areas: verify insurance eligibility 48–72 hours before every appointment to prevent the most common claim denials; collect patient copays and estimated balances at the time of service before the patient leaves the chair; and submit clean claims electronically within 24 hours of treatment. Practices that tighten all three consistently improve collection rates by 3–6 percentage points within 90 days without adding headcount. What is a good collection rate for a solo dental practice? A good collection rate for a solo dental practice is 98% or higher of adjusted net production. The industry average is 91–95% , but practices consistently below 95% have a systemic billing problem worth investigating immediately. Every 1% below 98% on an $800,000 practice represents approximately $8,000 in annual revenue loss that has already been earned but never collected. How Many AR Days Should a Dental Practice Target? AR days should be under 30 days for a healthy solo dental practice. Best-in-class practices run 25 days or fewer. AR days above 45 indicate a breakdown in denial follow-up, payment posting, or patient balance collection. The ADA recommends addressing overdue accounts with a written financial policy and consistent follow-up procedures at defined intervals. How Do I Reduce AR in My Solo Dental Practice? To reduce accounts receivable in a solo dental office collections system, focus on three areas: Prevent upstream errors — verify insurance eligibility 48–72 hours before every appointment and submit clean claims within 24 hours of service Collect at the time of service — patient balance collection drops approximately 20% once a patient has left. Collect before they get up from the chair. Follow up on a defined schedule — use the 90-day AR calendar above with specific actions at Day 7, 14, 30, 45, 60, and 90 after service What percentage of dental insurance claims are denied? Approximately 15–20% of dental insurance claims are denied on first submission. A denial rate above 15% signals systemic issues in eligibility verification, coding, or documentation, according to dental claim data . The more consequential figure: according to Beckers Healthcare , 65% of denied claims are never resubmitted, representing permanent revenue loss rather than a timing delay. Billing Tools and Process Should a solo dentist outsource billing? Outsourcing billing makes sense in four situations: AR days consistently exceed 45, denial rate is above 15%, AR90+ is above 5% of total AR , or you have no dedicated billing staff. These are the industry-standard trigger thresholds. For practices with experienced in-house billing and denial rates under 10%, AI automation tools can provide comparable efficiency improvements. Reduced errors, automated verification, systematic follow-up — without the cost premium or communication friction of a third-party billing company. What is a clean claim rate in dental billing? A clean claim is a dental insurance claim submitted without errors, with all required documentation attached. The payer can adjudicate it without requesting additional information. Your clean claim rate is the percentage of claims paid on first submission — no corrections, no follow-up needed. A 95% clean claim rate is the benchmark for healthy solo dental practice collections. Practices above that threshold collect faster. Payers process clean claims with significantly shorter turnaround times. How does an AI receptionist help with dental collections? An AI receptionist like Arini improves collections upstream by capturing patient insurance information during the scheduling call — before the appointment, before the claim is filed. That data flows directly to your PMS (OpenDental, EagleSoft, Denticon, and other systems). It reduces eligibility verification errors, which account for 35% of claim denials . Arini also handles incoming call volume 24/7. Your front desk can focus on AR follow-up and claim appeals instead of answering the phone. Learn more at arini.ai . When should a dental practice send accounts to collections? A dental practice should consider third-party collections when a patient balance remains unpaid past 90 days. Specifically: two statements sent, at least one direct outreach attempt made, the patient is unresponsive, and no payment plan is in place. The ADA provides guidance on overdue accounts , including recommended language for financial policies and past-due notices. Before sending to collections, make a documented final phone call. Many practices recover balances with direct outreach at far lower cost than a collection agency. Conclusion: Build a System, Not Just a Policy The most impactful shift solo dental practice owners can make is moving from reactive billing to a proactive collections system. The six mistakes outlined in this guide aren't failures of effort. They're failures of process. When the verification sequence is defined, the 90-day calendar is followed, and monthly metrics are reviewed, collections becomes predictable cash flow. Not a chronic problem. For most solo practices, the highest-ROI move isn't hiring an additional billing specialist or outsourcing everything. It's building better upstream systems that prevent denials before they happen, combined with tools that free your existing team to focus on AR management instead of call volume. title: Jennifer Claman is Building Gynovent to Design Women's Health Devices That Put Patients First
summary: Many women's health devices aren't designed with the patient's experience in mind. That's why Jennifer Claman is building Gynovent, a women’s health medical device company built to create innovative products that women truly want and physicians genuinely need.
body_text: Women’s health is one of the most underserved areas in medicine and one of the most underfunded in venture. Just 2% of VC funding is invested in women's health, and only half of that goes to female founders. But many of the tools used in women’s health are in drastic need of innovation. The vaginal speculum, in particular, is used on roughly 60 million female patients a year in the US, but was never designed with patient comfort in mind and has gone largely unchanged in over 150 years. Having spent 30 years as a full-scope OB/GYN, Dr. Jennifer Claman was tired of depending on outdated tools. So she set out to launch Gynovent and redesign the speculum and other women’s health devices to finally put patients and providers first. Introducing Gynovent: Empowering innovation, revolutionizing wellness Gynovent is a women’s health medical device company built to create innovative products that women truly want and physicians genuinely need. The team’s lead product is a completely redesigned vaginal speculum—the standard device used in every screening and pelvic exam. “The device we currently use,” Jennifer explains, “was developed during the Civil War-era and hasn't really gotten an overhaul. Clearly there was absolutely no attention to the comfort and well-being of the patient in that design.” Gynovent is taking a different approach. By offering color options, self-insertion, and an optional mirror, the team is centering their redesign around the patient experience. "We've been trying to shove a square peg in a round hole for nearly 200 years,” Jennifer says. “At least let's put a round peg in there." By introducing products that improve patient well-being and the practitioner experience, Jennifer aims to pave the way for more mission-driven funds focused on health, grounded in the belief that “the most effective way to raise money in this space is to create really good products that are going to help a lot of people." Jennifer’s journey to Gynovent Before her founder journey, Jennifer spent 30 years as a full-scope OB/GYN, working as a referral surgeon for some of the most complicated gynecologic surgeries in the LA basin. Alongside clinical work, Jennifer spent 15 years as co-chair of Kaiser Permanente ’s national new-product evaluation and approval committee in the OB/GYN space, gaining firsthand insight into medical device approval processes. Throughout decades of practicing, Jennifer worked hard to bring new innovations into the women’s health space, but was regularly restricted by the challenges that occur within hospitals and with payers who do not prioritize women’s health, which is often reimbursed at lower levels than other sectors of medicine. Women’s health devices regularly left patients uncomfortable and disempowered, and Jennifer saw many patients miss preventative screening exams because they'd viewed them as too uncomfortable, only to end up with advanced conditions down the line. Though Jennifer had instilled the motto of “don’t complain about things, just change them,” in her family household, it wasn’t until Jennifer’s daughters asked her, “if you don’t like it, why don’t you just change it?” that Jennifer knew she’d have to build better women’s health devices herself. She stepped away from full-time practice and launched Gynovent, focusing first on redesigning the speculum, as it's the entry point to gynecologic care for the majority of women. The fact that there has been virtually no innovation in the device in over 150 years is indicative of the attitude of society towards women’s health, Jennifer believes. "What we fail to improve reveals what we fail to value." Just over a year later, Gynovent’s prototype speculum has been evaluated by providers responsible for contracting decisions at several major health plans, and the team has received letters of interest from Kaiser , UCLA , the VA , and Sutter Health . Jennifer is currently focused on raising Gynovent’s angel round. Jennifer’s Advice for Fellow Founders Founder education is critical, Jennifer says, particularly early in the journey. “Educate yourself at the very beginning, before you take too many steps, about the best way to travel your road, and learn what areas are most likely to result in successful outcomes.” In her own experience, Jennifer found that it’s critical to tailor your education, expectations, and goals to your category—as building is different in every sector. “When I started, I tried pitching to some big venture capitalists. But Med Tech, especially women's Med Tech, can't compete against an AI-driven company run by three 25-year-olds that has no cost to infrastructure and a potential $30 billion upside. I needed to be in the room with the people who are interested in Med Tech from the beginning. That simple, pretty obvious lesson probably took me eight months to figure out." To learn more about Jennifer’s founder journey, you can follow her on LinkedIn and visit gynovent.com .

title: Automating modern governance: Triggering access certifications with Okta Identity Threat Protection Workflows
summary: Learn how to trigger real-time access certifications using Okta Identity Threat Protection and Okta Workflows to automate risk-based identity governance.
body_text: TL;DR: By combining Okta Identity Threat Protection with Okta Workflows, organizations can transition from static, scheduled access reviews to dynamic, real-time access certifications based on user risk, ensuring immediate remediation of potential threats. Managing identity governance often relies on scheduled campaigns—typically quarterly or annually—to ensure users have appropriate access levels. But in today's fast-paced threat landscape, waiting for the end of the quarter to review a compromised or risky user just doesn't cut it. What if you could trigger an access review the exact moment a threat is detected? By combining Okta Identity Threat Protection with Okta Workflows , you can move from static, scheduled reviews to dynamic, real-time access certifications based on user risk. Instead of just reviewing access when the calendar dictates, you can review it exactly when a threat profile changes. The architecture: From real-time risk to policy-driven action Before exploring specific features, here is a high-level look at how real-time risk signals seamlessly flow into policy-driven governance actions. The real-time risk architecture pipeline Flowchart of real-time risk signals from Okta Identity Threat Detection triggering dynamic certification campaigns to Okta Workflows. Fill out the form to access this content. To understand how these systems communicate, here’s the technical sequence of the automated governance loop: Risk ingestion: Okta Identity Threat Protection evaluates continuous risk signals via first-party behavioral analytics or third-party vendors. Event triggers: An entity risk level change (like from low to high) fires an asynchronous event hook in Okta. Workflow orchestration: Okta Workflows captures the event via the “Risk Level Changed” trigger card. Context enrichment and evaluation: The workflow executes logic checks, fetches user attributes, and evaluates the risk context. Governance execution: If conditions are met, the workflow invokes the Okta Identity Governance API to instantly spin up a targeted micro-campaign for that specific user ID. Key capabilities of the Okta governance engine Here are three features from Okta's governance engine that make this modern approach a total game-changer. 1. Dynamic certification campaigns triggered by risk This is where the true magic of automation happens. Instead of relying solely on a schedule, Okta Workflows lets you dynamically generate a targeted access certification campaign. A workflow initiates instantly when a user’s risk profile elevates. This can happen due to a session hijacking attempt detected by Okta’s first-party signals or a shared signal from an external security provider. The workflow evaluates the user's risk level. If it identifies a high risk, Okta automatically launches a "Risky User Campaign" specifically for that individual and immediately pings your security team in a Slack channel. You get an instant, targeted security review exactly when it matters most. 2. Deep context for reviewers (hello, software rationalization!) Reviewers, such as managers or resource owners, need actionable data rather than a blind list of applications when alerted to review a risky user. Okta’s Governance Analyzer provides incredible context so they can make an informed, confident decision. One standout feature is the license utilization data. For instance, the review dashboard might flag a user who has a Microsoft Office 365 license but hasn't actually logged in for the past 90 days. This not only shrinks the attack surface from a security perspective but is also a massive win for software rationalization. You can easily spot and revoke unused licenses, saving your organization significant money in the process. 3. Built-in separation of duties checks Access reviews aren't just about whether a user needs access; they must evaluate whether that access creates a toxic combination. The Okta review dashboard automatically runs checks against your organization's separation of duties (SoD) policies. For example, if a risky user holds both "user administrator" and "billing administrator" roles, the platform immediately flags this SoD conflict for the reviewer. Coupled with machine learning-driven recommendations on whether to approve or revoke access, reviewers are perfectly equipped to mitigate compliance risks on the spot. Ready to build it yourself? title: Visitor Management System Buying Guide: What Facilities Teams Should Look For in 2026
summary: Security, compliance, integrations, and the questions to ask every VMS vendor in 2026.
body_text: What facilities teams should look for in a visitor management system in 2026 — security, compliance, integrations, and the questions to ask vendors. Choosing a visitor management system used to be a simple checkbox: can it print a badge? In 2026, facilities and security teams are evaluating visitor management as part of a broader building security and compliance stack — which means the buying criteria have gotten a lot more specific. Here's what to actually look for, and the questions worth asking every vendor on your shortlist. What Is a Visitor Management System? A visitor management system (VMS) replaces the paper sign-in sheet with a digital process for registering, badging, tracking, and checking out guests, contractors, and other non-employees who enter a facility. Modern systems also handle pre-registration, host notifications, safety acknowledgments, and real-time on-site visibility. Why This Decision Matters More Than It Used To Facilities teams are no longer just managing front-desk convenience — they're managing liability. Real-time dashboards showing who's on-site, where they're supposed to be, and how long they've been there have become critical for emergency response and safety-regulation compliance, not just a nice-to-have front-desk feature. What to Look For in a Visitor Management System 1. Real-time visibility You should be able to see, at any moment, exactly who is currently on-site — not just who checked in that day. This matters most during an emergency evacuation, when knowing who's actually in the building is the whole point. 2. A real check-out process A surprising number of systems handle check-in well and check-out poorly. Visitors should be able to check out via kiosk, mobile, or a staff-assisted flow — otherwise your "who's on-site" data is wrong by the end of every day. 3. Integration with access control and badge systems The best visitor management setups don't operate in isolation — they connect to your access control, CCTV, and alarm systems so a visitor badge can actually restrict where someone can go, and security events tie back to visitor records automatically. 4. Data-driven visitor insights Look for analytics on peak visitor times, frequent guests, and average visit duration. That data helps facilities teams plan front-desk staffing and spot unusual patterns that might indicate a security risk — not just a report nobody reads. 5. Compliance and documentation features For regulated industries or multi-site organizations, look for the ability to tailor sign-in documents by visitor type, enforce re-acknowledgment of safety policies on a set cadence, automatically store signed agreements, and optionally require a short safety video or quiz before badge issuance. 6. Cloud-based and remotely manageable Cloud-hosted systems let facilities and security teams manage settings, pull reports, and respond to on-site events remotely — important for any organization managing more than one location. Questions to Ask Vendors Does the system support both check-in and check-out, and how is check-out enforced in practice? What access control and security systems does it integrate with out of the box? Can visitor types (contractor, guest, vendor) have different sign-in flows and document requirements? What visitor analytics and reporting come standard, and can they be filtered by location? How is visitor data stored, for how long, and does that meet our compliance requirements? How Visitor Management Fits Into a Broader Workplace Platform The most efficient setups don't treat visitor management as a standalone tool — they connect it to the same platform handling desk booking, room scheduling, and badge access, so a visitor's host, meeting room, and building access are all tied together automatically. See how Zynq's visitor management integrates with desk and room booking, or read about the shift toward a single workplace operating system . Frequently Asked Questions What should facilities teams look for in a visitor management system? The core criteria are real-time on-site visibility, a genuine check-out process, integration with access control and security systems, visitor analytics, and compliance and documentation features — particularly for regulated industries or multi-site organizations. Do visitor management systems integrate with access control? The strongest systems do — linking visitor badges to access control, CCTV, and alarm systems so a visitor's building access is automatically restricted to where they're supposed to be, and security events tie back to their visit record. Is cloud-based visitor management better than on-premise? For most multi-location organizations, yes — cloud-based systems allow facilities and security teams to manage settings and pull reports remotely, and they typically support easier integration with other cloud-based security tools. title: Testing full-duplex voice agents: what changes when your model listens and speaks at once
summary: GPT-Live made full-duplex the default. Here's what breaks in your voice-agent eval stack, and what audio-native testing has to look like now.
body_text: On July 8, OpenAI shipped GPT-Live , a new generation of voice models built on a full-duplex architecture that can listen and speak at the same time. During a conversation the model can backchannel with "mhmm" or "yeah", stay quiet while you think, and delegate hard reasoning to GPT-5.5 in the background while the conversation keeps flowing. The API access is described as coming soon , but the direction is clear enough: full-duplex is quickly becoming the default assumption for what a voice agent feels like. For anyone running production voice agents, this is also the moment your eval stack goes half-blind. A test harness built around transcripts, text loopbacks, and strict half-duplex turn boundaries cannot see the failure modes a full-duplex agent actually produces. That gap is what this post is about: what full-duplex changes at the architecture level, why transcript-based evaluation stops working, and what it takes to test these agents before your callers do. What full-duplex actually changes The previous generation of voice systems, including OpenAI's own Advanced Voice Mode, still operated through discrete turns. <cite index="29-3,29-4,29-5">The model had to wait for the user to stop speaking before responding, and because turn detection is based on silence, even a brief pause or background noise could be mistaken for the end of turn, causing the model to interrupt at unnatural times.</cite> GPT-Live throws that pipeline out. <cite index="29-8,29-9">Instead of processing a sequence of separate messages, GPT-Live continuously processes input while generating output, and the model can make interaction decisions many times per second: whether to speak, continue listening, pause, interrupt, or invoke a tool.</cite> There is no single "end of user turn" event anymore. There is a continuous loop of micro-decisions. Three things fall out of that architecture that matter for testing: Backchannels become first-class outputs. The agent emits short cues like "mhmm" and "got it" while the user is still talking . Those tokens never make it into a clean speaker-separated transcript the way a normal reply does. Silence is signal, not turn-end. <cite index="23-5,23-6">The model can produce backchannel responses like "mhmm" or "yeah" while you're still speaking, handle pauses without interpreting them as turn-endings, and users can explicitly tell it to stay silent by saying something like "just hold on".</cite> Reasoning is decoupled from voicing. <cite index="22-18,22-19,22-20,22-21">OpenAI decoupled continuous interaction from heavier reasoning, so when a task needs search, reasoning, or more agentic capabilities, GPT-Live delegates it to another model such as GPT-5.5 in the background, while GPT-Live keeps the conversation flowing.</cite> That "keeps the conversation flowing" part is where new failure modes live. How a full-duplex agent decides, many times per second This is not just an OpenAI change. LiveKit shipped adaptive interruption handling whose <cite index="36-9">adaptive interruption model is trained on real conversational audio to distinguish true interruption attempts from non-interruptive speech</cite>. Research benchmarks like Full-Duplex-Bench-v2 and τ-Voice exist because <cite index="17-6">when full-duplex systems are tested, they often get confused when people talk at the same time, struggle to handle corrections smoothly, and sometimes lose track of who or what is being talked about</cite>. The problem is industry-wide, and it is empirical. The failure modes text can't see Here is a partial catalogue of things that go wrong in a full-duplex agent and are essentially invisible in a transcript diff: Talk-over. The agent starts speaking during a real user statement, not a pause. In a written transcript both turns look fine; on the audio you hear one voice on top of another. Mis-timed backchannels. Simon Willison described an early GPT-Live bug where <cite index="24-2">the model was "interrupting me and laughing at my (not really intended as) jokes while I was still talking"</cite>. That laugh is a two-hundred-millisecond audio artifact in the middle of the user's turn. It is not a "wrong answer" any semantic eval can catch. False barge-ins. A TV in the next room, a passing siren, or a stray "uh-huh" from the caller trips the agent into cancelling its own reply and restarting from silence. The transcript shows a truncated agent turn followed by a new one. It looks fine on paper; on the phone it feels broken. Delegation stalls. The foreground model routes a hard question to the background reasoner and, if not tuned right, goes uncannily silent instead of filling the wait with a natural "let me check that for you". The transcript records the eventual correct answer. It does not record the four seconds of dead air that made the caller hang up. Endpoint hallucinations. A caller pauses to breathe. The agent decides they are done, cuts them off, answers the half-question, and now the whole conversation is off the rails. Every one of these is a sound problem, not a text problem. And every one of these is exactly the class of failure full-duplex architectures create more of, not less. <cite index="25-1">Full-duplex invites its own new failure mode, a model that talks over you when it thinks it heard a backchannel.</cite> Why the old eval stack breaks Most voice-agent test harnesses today do one of three things: Diff a transcript against a golden transcript. Run a text loopback: feed prompts to the LLM part of the stack, score the text out. Run a turn-based simulator that alternates cleanly: user says X, agent says Y, user says Z. Each of these was reasonable when the underlying architecture was a cascade of STT into an LLM into TTS with strict turn boundaries. None of them survives contact with full-duplex. A transcript diff cannot represent overlapping audio. The best it can do is note that agent tokens and user tokens have interleaved timestamps, and that is not the same as knowing whether the caller heard the agent talking over them. A text loopback skips the entire audio path, which means it skips VAD, endpointing, echo cancellation, TTS cancel-on-interrupt, and every timing-sensitive decision the agent actually makes on a phone call. A turn-based simulator, by construction, cannot produce the overlap conditions that make full-duplex agents fail. The point Evalgent made recently is blunt and correct: <cite index="12-9,12-10,12-11">full-duplex moves the hardest behaviour into turn-taking, and turn-taking is invisible to text-based testing; you cannot catch a talk-over by reading a transcript, you have to test over real audio, with overlapping speech and interruptions built in.</cite> Old eval stack vs what full-duplex requires What audio-native testing actually requires If you take the failure catalogue seriously, the requirements for a real eval harness fall out fairly cleanly: Real audio path, not a text shortcut. Your test callers need to speak to your agent over the same transport your users do. For phone-based agents that means PSTN. For embedded or browser agents that means WebRTC. Anything less bypasses the parts of the stack that matter. Synthetic callers with configurable overlap behavior. You need to be able to say "this caller barges in aggressively", "this one pauses mid-sentence to think", "this one backchannels with 'right, right'". If you cannot programmatically produce a caller who talks over your agent, you cannot regression-test talk-over recovery. Audio-native metrics. You need scores that come from the sound of the call, not from the transcript. That means metrics for interruption timing, talk-over rate, backchannel appropriateness, latency to first token after end-of-turn, silence gap distribution, pronunciation of proper nouns. LiveKit's own documentation makes the point: <cite index="36-1">an agent session collects interruption metrics for each barge-in detection, including per-event latency, and the number of requests and interruptions.</cite> Those numbers only exist if you are looking at the audio. Persona diversity. Different accents, different speech pace, different background noise, different languages. The failure surface of a full-duplex agent is not uniform across those axes; a Silero VAD tuned for clean American English will endpoint differently on a caller with a heavy accent in a moving car. Regression suites, not one-off runs. Full-duplex behavior is unstable in a specific way: the same code shipped against a new hosted model version will fail differently. You need to be able to replay a specific past interaction against a new build and see what changed. This is exactly what we built Roark for. Roark's simulation testing dials your voice agent over real phone calls or WebRTC, drives the call from a persona with a distinct voice, accent, pace, emotional register and background noise, and scores what came back with audio-native metrics for interruptions, pace and pauses, vocal stress, and 60+ others. Simulations are built from personas, scenarios, run plans, and schedules, so recurring runs can gate CI over HTTP. There are one-click integrations for Vapi, Retell, LiveKit, Pipecat, Bland, and ElevenLabs . Simulating a full-duplex agent before launch The concrete pre-launch loop looks something like this. Define a small set of personas that stress the parts of the pipeline you think are most fragile: personas: - id: aggressive_barge_in voice: en-US-female-fast behavior: barge_in_probability: 0.6 mid_utterance_pauses: rare background_noise: none - id: thoughtful_pauser voice: en-GB-male-slow behavior: barge_in_probability: 0.0 mid_utterance_pauses: frequent # 800ms - 2s backchannels: ["mhmm", "right"] - id: noisy_environment voice: es-MX-female-medium behavior: barge_in_probability: 0.2 background_noise: coffee_shop accent_strength: 0.8 Then build scenarios that exercise a specific decision path. An outbound sales agent might have "caller asks the same question three times", "caller interrupts the pitch to ask price", "caller says 'hold on' mid-answer". Each scenario becomes a scored run. The output is a suite result, not a single number: Illustrative pre-launch simulation suite result Two things are worth pointing out about this loop. First, most of the value shows up when you look at the failed calls , not the aggregate score. A pass rate on a full-duplex suite is a lagging indicator; the actual signal is in the specific rows where the agent talked over the caller for 3.8 seconds or endpointed on a natural in-breath. Second, the persona list is where taste matters. A hundred easy calls tell you nothing. Ten hard, diverse calls tell you everything. Regression when the model changes underneath you Full-duplex agents built on hosted foundation models have a specific operational problem: the model changes and you find out about it in production. OpenAI has said <cite index="22-22">GPT-Live is designed so it can adopt newer frontier models as they ship.</cite> That is a nice property for capability. It is a hostile property for stability. If you are wiring your production stack to a hosted realtime model (OpenAI's Realtime API, xAI's Grok Voice , Gemini Live, or one of the platform-level products from Vapi or Retell that sit on top of them), the model version you launched against will not be the model version live traffic hits next month. Sometimes the change is announced. Often it is not. Either way, your talk-over rate can shift overnight. The mitigations that actually work are boring: Version-pin where you can. Where the underlying model exposes a stable version, pin it and upgrade deliberately. Replay real production calls against every candidate build. Capture what happened yesterday. Play it back against tomorrow's stack. Diff the audio-native scores. This is where Roark's production call replay earns its keep: real failed calls become the regression suite that guards future launches. Score every live call, not a 1% sample. With full-duplex, the pathological calls are individually rare and collectively frequent. A random sample will miss the interesting ones. Score everything, file issues on threshold breaches, and let a human triage the filed queue. Illustrative Roark call review, full-duplex agent What to do this week If you are shipping a voice agent right now, treat GPT-Live as a signal that the ground under your test harness moved: Audit what your evals actually see. If your regression suite is text-based, note it. That is not evidence your agent works; it is evidence your evals cannot fail. Add three overlap scenarios by end of week. Aggressive barge-in, mid-utterance pauser, noisy background. Run them on your current build. The failures will not be subtle. Turn every production incident into a regression test. The next talk-over complaint you get should end up as a replayable scenario you run before every deploy. Score interruption metrics, not just task success. Per-event barge-in latency, talk-over duration, endpoint-hallucination rate. Track them over builds. Full-duplex is a genuine step forward for how voice agents feel to talk to. It is also the point at which "vibes-based QA plus a few golden transcripts" stops being a defensible position. The teams that adapt first will notice, because their launch weeks get quiet. The teams that do not will notice too, because their callers will tell them, one talk-over at a time.

title: Kristian Ranta has always been talking openly about suicide — and now, Meru Health helps prevent it
summary: At Meru Health, our CEO Kristian Ranta has always been willing to share his story.
body_text: At Meru Health, our CEO Kristian Ranta has always been willing to share his story. Kristian lost his brother Peter to suicide in 2005 after decades of struggling with depression. “For years, I wondered why he could not be treated effectively and how people like him could be helped in the future, before it’s too late,” says Kristian. Losing his brother—who taught him philosophy and his appreciation for classical music—spurred Kristian into action. He’s has been spreading awareness about suicide ever since. Even though taboo still keeps many people from openly discussing suicide, the stats are staggering. According to the CDC, the percentage of adults with recent symptoms of an anxiety or a depressive disorder increased from 36.4% to 41.5% during a recent stretch of the pandemic (August 2020–February 2021).1 In the United States, we lost 47,511 people to suicide in 2019—that’s about 14.5 in every 100,000 people.2 Suicide is the second leading cause of death among people between the ages of 10 and 34.3 Kristian’s brother Peter struggled for decades with depression. None of the treatment options available, like antidepressant medications, seemed to help. Kristian founded Meru Health in 2016, with a mission to empower 10 million people suffering from mental health challenges by 2027 — and to ensure that people like Peter get the care and support they need. At Meru Health, we’ve created a clinically proven treatment program for depression, anxiety, and burnout with long-lasting outcomes. It’s always been Kristian’s goal to ensure that using this program not only reduces anxiety and depression symptoms, but also prevents suicide. Our latest research study (currently under peer-review) suggests that the Meru Health Program has reached that goal. The program is estimated to prevent 1 suicide attempt for every 438 patients it enrolls, and preventing 1 death by suicide for every 5841 patients enrolled. By those estimates, if our results generalized to everyone with a past-year major depressive episode in the United States in 2019, enrollment in Meru Health’s program might have prevented up to 44,194 suicide attempts, and saved up to 3,314 lives. The program is estimated to prevent 1 suicide attempt for every 438 patients it enrolls, and preventing 1 death by suicide for every 5841 patients enrolled. Our team at Meru Health is going to keep pushing. As mentioned, the findings about Meru Health Program’s suicide prevention are being peer-reviewed. Earlier this year, we published a study proving that our mobile health program effectively reduces symptoms of severe depression, with long-lasting results. The Meru Health coaching program is intended to help people navigate early signs of depression, anxiety, and burnout, to prevent those symptoms from progressing. Kristian says, “We know Meru Health can save lives and I want to keep any other family from going through what we did. We’ve built an effective, accessible treatment and we’re going to reach as many people as we can.” By the year 2030, it’s projected that “mental health problems (particularly depression) will be the leading cause of mortality and morbidity globally.”4 This September, during Suicide Prevention Awareness Month , Kristian and our team at Meru Health are continuing to speak openly about depression and suicide, and how we can reach individuals when they need it most with accessible, effective care. As Kristen Routh (PsyD, LMFT) shared, “The big takeaway is that people look at [suicide] as a stigma, like “let’s not talk about it because it might push people to do it.” In fact, the research shows the opposite — the more you talk about it, the more people are open to discuss their struggles.” When Kristian started opening up about his family’s loss, he says, “Talking about suicide felt like a huge taboo. But when I started sharing my story, I realized how many people had gone through something similar in their own family or community.” We need to follow Kristian’s example of speaking openly about how many of our loved ones are dying by suicide — and how we can reach people earlier on with the quality care and support they need. If in immediate danger, call suicide hotline The National Suicide Prevention Lifeline: 1-800-273-8255 The Trevor Lifeline (dedicated to helping LGBTQ+ youth in crisis): 1-866-488-7386 Trans Lifeline (peer support for transgender and questioning people): 1-877-330-6366 Veterans Crisis Line: 1-800-273-8255 and press 1
